unique_missions.description: BARREL-1K was a NASA/Dartmouth high-altitude balloon payload flown in the first BARREL Antarctic campaign in 2013, with the flight ending in 2013. It drifted in the Antarctic stratosphere/polar vortex rather than orbiting Earth, at roughly 30–40 km altitude over Antarctica and the Southern Ocean, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays and magnetic fields from radiation-belt electron precipitation.

San Antonio Geophysical Observatory was a fixed ground-based geomagnetic/magnetometer station in San Antonio, Texas, with CDAWeb holdings from at least the International Geophysical Year era (1957; exact start/end not clear in registry metadata). It recorded local geomagnetic-field variations for magnetospheric, ionospheric, geomagnetic-storm, and space-weather studies.

Bay Mills Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetic station at Bay Mills, Michigan, USA, used for heliophysics and space-weather studies of geomagnetic and ionospheric current systems. It has no orbit; it measures local geomagnetic field variations with a magnetometer. Exact operational start/end years are not confirmed in the supplied SPASE/CDAWeb summary.

CSSWE (Colorado Student Space Weather Experiment) was a 3U CubeSat launched in 2012 and operated until 2014 in a single low-Earth orbit, about 480 x 780 km at 65° inclination, with gradual orbital decay rather than planned relocations. Its REPTile telescope measured energetic radiation-belt electrons and protons to study space-weather-driven particle dynamics.

BARREL-2E was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses payload, launched and operated only during its 2014 Antarctic long-duration stratospheric balloon flight. Drifting over Antarctica rather than orbiting, it measured bremsstrahlung X rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetic-field, GPS, and housekeeping data for conjunctions with the Van Allen Probes.

PENGUIn-0 (PG0) is a ground geophysical observatory at/near Amundsen–Scott South Pole Station, Antarctica, operational by the 2010s, measuring geomagnetic field variations with a magnetometer for polar ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies; it is a fixed ground site, not an orbital mission.

The Lovozero (LOV) magnetometer is a ground-based geomagnetic station at Lovozero on Russia’s Kola Peninsula (~68.0°N, 35.0°E), operating by the early 1990s and contributing to the IMAGE/IAGA network. It measures ground magnetic-field variations for auroral, ionospheric-current, substorm, and magnetosphere–ionosphere coupling studies; it has no orbital phases.

Maniitsoq Geophysical Observatory has operated at Maniitsoq, formerly Sukkertoppen, on Greenland’s west coast since about 1972–1973; it is a fixed ground station with no orbit. It records local geomagnetic field variations with ground magnetometers for auroral electrojet, ionospheric current, magnetic storm, and magnetospheric studies.

NOAA-10 was a NOAA POES/TIROS-N polar-orbiting environmental satellite (launched 1986; operational to 1991) in a near-circular Sun-synchronous low-Earth orbit at about 800–850 km and 98–99° inclination; its orbit did not have distinct science phases. Its SEM package measured precipitating/trapped energetic electrons and protons for radiation-belt, auroral, and space-weather studies.

NASA’s Wind spacecraft (launched 1994) studies solar wind plasma, magnetic fields, energetic particles, and radio/plasma waves. From 1994 to 2004 it flew evolving highly elliptical Earth orbits with lunar swingbys, magnetosphere/radiation-belt crossings, and deep magnetotail excursions; since 2004 it has operated in a halo orbit around Sun–Earth L1 monitoring the upstream solar wind.

Karmøy Geophysical Observatory (Karmøy, Norway; magnetometer operations began in 1983 and continue in the CDAWeb/SMWG record, with exact end/status not independently confirmed) is a fixed ground station measuring local geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric current, substorm, geomagnetic-storm, and magnetospheric studies; it has no orbital phases.

Summit Geophysical Observatory is a ground station at Summit Station on the Greenland ice sheet, operating since at least 1997 in CDAWeb records. It provides fixed high-latitude geomagnetic measurements, chiefly fluxgate magnetometer observations of field variations, for studies of auroral electrodynamics, ionospheric currents, and magnetospheric disturbances; its location has not changed.

BARREL-1B was one payload in NASA’s Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses, operated during the 2013 Antarctic long-duration balloon campaign. Flying in the stratosphere over Antarctica rather than in orbit, it measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer and GPS/ephemeris data for geospace context.

The Gakona Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground site near Gakona, Alaska, USA, operational since the late 1990s and represented in CDAWeb for ground magnetometer data. It measures local geomagnetic field variations from auroral electrojets, ionospheric currents, and magnetospheric disturbances; as a ground station it has no orbital phases or changing vantage point.

Harris Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground geomagnetic station near Harris, Minnesota, USA (operational start/end not clearly documented in SPASE/CDAWeb). It measures local variations in Earth’s magnetic field with a magnetometer for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and geomagnetic-pulsation studies; its observing vantage point does not change.

ESA/NASA’s Solar Orbiter (launched 2020) studies the Sun and inner heliosphere with remote-sensing imagers/spectrometers and in-situ plasma, fields and particle instruments. It has always been in heliocentric orbit: 2020-2021 was cruise/commissioning with Venus flybys in Dec 2020 and Aug 2021 and an Earth flyby in Nov 2021; since late 2021 it has used repeated Venus assists to lower perihelion toward ~0.28 AU and raise inclination for out-of-ecliptic solar views.

Pangnirtung Geophysical Observatory, operational since about 1993, is a ground geomagnetic station at Pangnirtung, Nunavut, Canada, not a spacecraft. It records geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for auroral-zone ionospheric and magnetospheric current studies and high-latitude space-weather research, contributing to Canadian geomagnetic data networks.

Bjorn is a ground geomagnetic observatory on Bjørnøya/Bear Island, Norway, in the high-latitude Arctic, hosting a magnetometer that records local geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies; its precise operational start/end dates and network affiliation are not confirmed in the supplied metadata.

McMath–Pierce Solar Telescope at Kitt Peak, Arizona, was a ground-based solar observatory operated from 1962 to 2017. It provided high-resolution visible and infrared observations of the Sun, especially spectroscopy of the photosphere, chromosphere, and sunspots; its Fourier Transform Spectrometer produced widely used detailed solar spectra.

Lucky Lake Magnetometer (IAGA LUC) is a ground-based geomagnetic observatory at Lucky Lake, Saskatchewan, Canada, operational by at least 2008 and apparently active in the INTERMAGNET/CANMOS era. It measures local vector geomagnetic field variations for magnetospheric, ionospheric, and space-weather studies; it has no orbital phases.

unique_missions.mission_name: Upgraded Very High Angular Resolution Ultraviolet Telescope (VAULT2.0)
unique_missions.description: VAULT/VAULT2.0 is a NASA sounding-rocket ultraviolet solar telescope, not an orbital observatory. Original VAULT suborbital flights from White Sands occurred in 1999 and 2002; the upgraded VAULT2.0 flew in 2014, with operations ending after each minutes-long flight. It obtained very high angular resolution H I Lyman-alpha 1216 Å solar images of the upper chromosphere and transition region.

GOES-16 (GOES-R), launched in 2016 and operational from 2017, is a NOAA geostationary satellite. It completed checkout near 89.5°W in 2016–2017, served as GOES-East near 75.2°W from Dec 2017 to Apr 2025, then moved to on-orbit standby/storage. It carries SUVI for full-disk solar EUV imaging plus EXIS, SEISS, and MAG for solar irradiance, energetic particles, and fields.

CANOPUS (Canadian Auroral Network for the OPEN Program Unified Study) was a Canadian ground-based auroral/geospace observatory network operated from 1986 to 2005 across subauroral and auroral latitudes in Canada. Its magnetometers, riometers, photometers, and all-sky imagers measured magnetic pulsations, cosmic-noise absorption, auroral emissions, and ionospheric activity; the magnetometer network continued as CARISMA.

Tasiilaq Geophysical Observatory is a ground geophysical/magnetic station in Tasiilaq, southeast Greenland, operated as part of Greenland geomagnetic monitoring and contributing data to CDAWeb. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies; it is a fixed ground site, not an orbiting mission. Operational start is not confidently verified here.

NASA's MAVEN (Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution; launched 2013, at Mars since 2014) studies Mars' upper atmosphere, ionosphere, solar-wind interaction, escape, plasma and magnetic fields. From 2014-2019 it flew a 4.5-hr highly elliptical Mars orbit (~150 x 6200 km, with periodic deep-dip campaigns to ~125 km); after 2019 aerobraking it has operated in a lower-apoapsis ~3.5-hr elliptical Mars orbit (~150 x 4500 km) while continuing science and relay support.

Gillam (IAGA GIM/GILL) is a fixed ground magnetometer observatory at Gillam, Manitoba, Canada, operational by the CANOPUS era in 1986 and continuing in CARISMA/INTERMAGNET service. It records vector geomagnetic-field variations for studies of auroral electrojets, substorms, ionospheric currents, and magnetospheric disturbances; its location has not changed.

Inukjuak Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground station at Inukjuak, Quebec, Canada, operational at least by the early 1990s and represented in CDAWeb for geomagnetic studies. It operates magnetometers measuring local geomagnetic field variations for auroral-ionospheric current and magnetospheric disturbance research as part of Canadian ground magnetic networks; it has no orbital or relocation phases.

Kuujjuarapik Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based heliophysics station at Kuujjuarapik, Quebec, Canada (near 55.3°N, 77.8°W). Operational in CDAWeb/THEMIS ground-magnetometer records from 2006 onward, it has no orbit; it measures local three-component geomagnetic field variations for studies of auroral currents, ionospheric electrodynamics, substorms, and magnetospheric activity.

Jackvik Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based magnetometer station at Jäckvik/Jackvik, northern Sweden, in the auroral-zone Scandinavian network, recording local geomagnetic-field variations for ionospheric current, substorm, ULF-wave, and magnetospheric studies. It has no orbit or relocation phases; registry start/end dates are not confirmed.

EUNIS is a NASA sounding-rocket solar spectrograph flown from White Sands Missile Range on suborbital flights since 2006, with solar campaigns including 2006, 2007, 2013, and 2021. It spends only minutes above the atmosphere per flight, observing high-resolution extreme-ultraviolet spectra/images of the chromosphere, transition region, and corona and calibrating space EUV instruments.

Fresno (IAGA code FRN) is a ground-based USGS geomagnetic observatory near Fresno/O’Neals, California, USA, operational since 1980. It has no orbit or changing vantage point; it continuously measures local vector geomagnetic field variations for studies of magnetic storms, ionospheric/magnetospheric currents, and secular change.

Worthington Geophysical Observatory was a ground magnetic observatory in Worthington, Minnesota, USA, operating at least in the late 20th-century CDAWeb/SPASE archive era; its exact start and end years are not confirmed here. It was not a spacecraft and had no orbital phases, measuring local geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for geomagnetic, ionospheric, and space-weather studies.

MetOp-B (launched 2012, operational 2013-present) is a EUMETSAT polar-orbiting meteorological satellite in a near-circular Sun-synchronous low Earth orbit at about 817 km altitude and 98.7° inclination; its orbit has not substantially changed. For heliophysics it carries NOAA SEM-2 sensors measuring energetic protons and electrons at satellite altitude for radiation belt and space-weather studies.

Interball-2 (Auroral Probe, launched 1996; science operations ended 1998) studied Earth’s auroral magnetosphere and ionosphere from a single highly elliptical, high-inclination Earth orbit, about 700–20,000 km altitude at ~63° inclination. It sampled auroral zones, polar cusp, and magnetospheric boundaries, measuring plasma, energetic particles, electric and magnetic fields, and waves.

Repulse Bay Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetic station at Repulse Bay/Naujaat, Nunavut, Canada, operating in CDAWeb-era records since at least the late 1980s. It has no orbit; it makes fixed-site high-latitude magnetometer measurements of geomagnetic-field variations used for auroral-zone, ionospheric current, substorm, and space-weather studies.

THEMIS-A (THA), launched in 2007, is a NASA THEMIS spacecraft for magnetospheric substorm studies. After launch and 2007 orbit phasing, it has remained in a highly elliptical, near-equatorial geocentric orbit sampling the inner/near-Earth magnetosphere and magnetotail, measuring electric and magnetic fields, plasma, and energetic particles with EFI, FGM/SCM, ESA, and SST; it was not transferred to lunar ARTEMIS.

Sakigake (MS-T5) was Japan/ISAS’s first deep-space probe (launched 1985; contact lost 1995), measuring interplanetary magnetic fields, solar-wind plasma waves, and energetic particles. It flew in heliocentric orbit after launch, passed Comet Halley in March 1986, then made an Earth gravity-assist flyby in January 1992 and continued on a revised heliocentric trajectory.

Cluster-Salsa (C2/FM6) was one of ESA’s four Cluster II spacecraft, launched in 2000 and operated until its controlled reentry in 2024. Throughout the mission it flew a highly elliptical polar Earth orbit in formation with the other Cluster spacecraft, with separations adjusted for multi-point sampling, to study the magnetosphere, bow shock, magnetopause, aurora, plasma particles, fields, and waves.

Trapper Creek Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetic station at Trapper Creek, Alaska, in operation in the THEMIS/CDAWeb era from at least the late 2000s. It measures local geomagnetic field variations with a ground magnetometer for studies of auroral-zone ionospheric currents and magnetospheric activity; it has no orbital or relocation phases.

Hornepayne Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetometer site at Hornepayne, Ontario, Canada, operational at least during CDAWeb holdings in the 2010s, measuring local geomagnetic-field variations for ionospheric current, substorm, and magnetospheric studies; it has no orbital or relocation phases.

Tucson (TUC) is a ground geomagnetic observatory near Tucson, Arizona, USA, operated in the IAGA/INTERMAGNET network since 1909 and available via CDAWeb. It has no orbit; fixed at its Arizona site, it records vector and scalar variations of Earth’s magnetic field with fluxgate/proton magnetometers for geomagnetic storms, ionospheric currents, and space-weather studies.

UCAR/NCAR HAO Historical Eclipse Archive (HXECLIPSE; VSO data service, operational start not documented here) is a virtual collection of ground-based solar eclipse photographs/images from HAO historical expeditions and other sources. It has no orbit or single station: observations were made from eclipse-path sites on Earth at the dates of individual eclipses, mainly of the white-light corona.

BARREL-1Q was a BARREL long-duration stratospheric balloon payload flown over Antarctica in early 2013, drifting in the polar vortex at about 30–40 km altitude. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, with magnetometer and GPS context, for magnetospheric space-weather studies coordinated with the Van Allen Probes.

Danmarkshavn Geophysical Observatory (DMH), operating since 1948, is a fixed ground magnetic observatory at Danmarkshavn in northeast Greenland. It measures local geomagnetic field variations with fluxgate/absolute magnetometers and provides high-latitude magnetic data for geomagnetic monitoring, auroral electrojet studies, and global observatory networks; it has no orbital phases.

Jan Mayen Magnetometer is a fixed ground geomagnetic observatory on Jan Mayen Island, Norway (about 70.9°N, 8.7°W), with IAGA/CDAWeb digital records in operation by at least the 1990s and continuing in modern archives. It measures vector geomagnetic field variations for high-latitude auroral, ionospheric, and magnetospheric studies.

ST5-224 was one of NASA’s three Space Technology 5 microsatellites, launched and operated in 2006 until mission end later that year. It flew a highly elliptical, near-polar low-Earth orbit, with no major orbital relocation, demonstrating nanosatellite constellation technologies while its miniature fluxgate magnetometer measured Earth’s magnetic field, auroral currents, and magnetospheric structure.

GOES-8 (launched 1994; operational 1995-2003) was a NOAA geostationary GOES-East satellite near 75°W longitude. It monitored Earth’s near-geosynchronous magnetospheric environment with magnetometer and energetic-particle sensors, plus space-weather solar X-ray observations; its science vantage remained geostationary until replacement and retirement in 2003.

LANL-2002 was a Los Alamos National Laboratory geosynchronous spacecraft operating from 2002 to 2008 at GEO, with no known major orbit change. It supported magnetospheric and space-weather studies; its Magnetospheric Plasma Analyzer (MPA) measured 3D ion and electron energy-per-charge distributions in the near-Earth plasma environment.

Oulujärvi (OUJ) is a fixed IAGA/IMAGE ground magnetometer station near Oulujärvi in central Finland, operational since 1983 with no orbital phases or relocations. It records three-component geomagnetic field variations for studies of auroral electrojets, ionospheric currents, geomagnetic pulsations, substorms, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling.

Hinode (Solar-B), launched in 2006 and still operating, is a JAXA/NASA/UK solar observatory in a near-circular Sun-synchronous low Earth polar orbit; its orbit has not substantially changed. It observes the solar photosphere, chromosphere, transition region, and corona, measuring magnetic fields, plasma dynamics, flares, eruptions, and coronal heating with SOT, XRT, and EIS.

Hi-C 2.1 (High Resolution Coronal Imager 2.1) was a NASA suborbital sounding-rocket solar observatory launched in 2018 from White Sands Missile Range; its mission ended after the same brief ballistic flight above Earth’s atmosphere. It obtained high-spatial-resolution 172 Å EUV images of active-region coronal loops and fine solar-corona structure.

Nordkapp Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground-based magnetometer station at Nordkapp, Norway, measuring local geomagnetic-field variations for high-latitude ionospheric, auroral-electrojet, and magnetospheric studies; no spacecraft orbit applies. Operational start/end are not confidently specified here.

NASA’s GOLD (Global-scale Observations of the Limb and Disk), launched in 2018 and in science operations since 2018, is a far-ultraviolet imaging spectrograph hosted on the SES-14 communications satellite in geostationary orbit near 47.5°W over the Americas. Its vantage has not changed; it images Earth’s thermosphere and ionosphere via disk and limb airglow.

ESA/NASA’s SOHO (launched Dec. 1995) is a solar/heliospheric observatory. After launch and transfer to the Sun-Earth L1 region in Dec. 1995-Feb. 1996, it has operated in a halo orbit about L1, observing the solar interior, photosphere, corona, CMEs, solar wind, and energetic particles with instruments such as LASCO, EIT, MDI, CELIAS, COSTEP, and ERNE.

Dynamics Explorer 2 (DE 2) was a NASA spacecraft launched in 1981 and operated until atmospheric reentry in 1983. It remained in a low-altitude, near-polar, elliptical Earth orbit (initially about 300–1000 km, decaying with time) to study ionosphere-thermosphere electrodynamics, measuring plasma, neutral winds/composition, electric and magnetic fields, and auroral current systems.

STEREO-A, launched in 2006, studies CMEs, solar eruptions, solar wind, energetic particles, and heliospheric structure with SECCHI, IMPACT, PLASTIC, and S/WAVES. After brief geocentric phasing orbits and a lunar gravity assist in Dec 2006, it entered a ~1 AU heliocentric orbit drifting ahead of Earth by about 22°/yr; it remained in this orbit through solar conjunction and returned near Earth in Aug 2023 after one full lap.

BARREL-4F (launched and ended in 2016) was a NASA BARREL high-altitude balloon payload from the fourth campaign, flown from the Esrange/Kiruna Arctic balloon base in Sweden rather than orbit. It drifted in the stratosphere measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, supporting studies of electron loss and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling.

Magion-4 was a Czech microsatellite of the Interball Tail Probe mission, launched in 1995 and operated until 1997. It flew the same highly elliptical geocentric magnetotail orbit throughout its life, with apogee near 200,000 km and perigee a few hundred km, sampling the magnetosphere, bow shock, magnetosheath, auroral/plasma regions, fields, waves, and energetic particles.

BARREL-2N was a NASA/Dartmouth stratospheric balloon payload launched and operated in the 2015 Northern Hemisphere BARREL campaign from Esrange/Kiruna, Sweden, drifting in the polar stratosphere. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetic-field and GPS/ephemeris data, to study magnetospheric loss processes.

Iqaluit (IQA) is a fixed ground-based IAGA/INTERMAGNET geomagnetic observatory at Iqaluit, Nunavut, Canada, with digital data available from 1992 and continuing. It measures local vector geomagnetic-field variations for auroral-zone ionospheric current, geomagnetic-storm, and magnetospheric studies; its observing location has not changed.

BARREL-1V was an individual NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload, launched and operated during the 2013 Antarctic stratospheric balloon campaign and ended after that flight. It drifted at long-duration-balloon altitudes over high southern latitudes, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons with magnetometer and GPS/ephemeris context.

Kiana Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetometer station at Kiana, Alaska, used in high-latitude magnetic monitoring networks. Operational since at least the 1990s, it measures local geomagnetic field variations for auroral ionosphere, magnetosphere, substorm, and current-system studies; as a fixed ground site it has no orbital phases.

Chibougamau Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetic station at Chibougamau, Quebec, Canada, operational by at least the 1990s in CDAWeb/SPASE ground magnetometer records. It measures geomagnetic field variations for auroral, ionospheric, and magnetospheric studies; as a ground observatory it has no orbital or vantage-point changes.

Clyde River Geophysical Observatory (operational by 1992; end not clearly specified in SPASE/CDAWeb records) is a fixed ground magnetometer site at Clyde River, Nunavut, Canada. It records geomagnetic field variations for high-latitude ionospheric, auroral, cusp, and magnetospheric studies.

Fort St. John Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetic observatory at Fort St. John, British Columbia, Canada, operated by Natural Resources Canada for heliophysics and space-weather studies. Since at least the late 20th century it has recorded local geomagnetic field variations with ground magnetometers; as a fixed ground site, it has no orbital phases.

NOAA GOES-14 (launched 2009, operated to 2020) was a geostationary Earth-orbit weather and space-environment satellite. It remained in geostationary orbit throughout, with checkout/storage and backup operations at changing longitudes, including around 105°W and temporary GOES-East service near 75°W in 2012–2013. EPS, MAG, and SEM/XRS monitored energetic particles, magnetic fields, and solar X-ray/EUV conditions.

BARREL-2Q was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL high-altitude balloon payload in the Antarctic stratosphere during the 2014 BARREL campaign, drifting with circumpolar winds rather than orbiting. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer and GPS/ephemeris data, for magnetospheric and space-weather studies.

Thule Air Base Geophysical Observatory at Pituffik/Thule, northwest Greenland, is a fixed high-Arctic ground observatory operating since at least the 1980s CDAWeb era. It measures local geomagnetic-field variations with a ground magnetometer to study polar-cap ionospheric currents, geomagnetic disturbances, and magnetosphere–ionosphere coupling; its observing location has not changed.

BARREL-3E was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload operated in 2015, launched from Esrange Space Center near Kiruna, Sweden for the northern high-latitude stratospheric balloon campaign. Floating in the Arctic stratosphere, it measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, plus magnetic field and GPS/ephemeris data.

ROCSAT-1 (FORMOSAT-1), Taiwan’s first satellite, operated from 1999 to 2004 in a low-Earth, near-circular orbit about 600 km altitude at 35° inclination; its orbit did not have distinct science phases. It studied the low-latitude/topside ionosphere and equatorial plasma electrodynamics, with IPEI measuring ion density, composition, temperature, and drift.

NASA’s Juno spacecraft (launched 2011) studies Jupiter’s interior, gravity/magnetic fields, aurorae, plasma, energetic particles, and radio/plasma waves. It cruised in heliocentric orbit from 2011-2016, including an Oct. 2013 Earth gravity assist, then entered a highly elliptical polar Jovian orbit in July 2016; its extended mission from 2021 used the evolving orbit for close Ganymede, Europa, and Io flybys while sampling Jupiter’s magnetosphere.

Masi Geophysical Observatory (IMAGE station MAS) is a ground magnetic station at Masi, Norway, operating since at least the modern IMAGE/CDAWeb era to record geomagnetic field variations with a fluxgate magnetometer for auroral ionosphere and magnetosphere studies; it has no orbit or relocation, serving as a fixed high-latitude station in the IMAGE magnetometer network.

BARREL-3G was an individual NASA BARREL stratospheric balloon payload operated in 2015 during the third long-duration balloon campaign from Esrange/Kiruna, Sweden, drifting at float altitude across the Arctic rather than orbiting. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, with GPS ephemeris and magnetic-field data.

BARREL-2B was a NASA Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload launched in the 2013-2014 Antarctic campaign and ended in 2014. It flew as a long-duration stratospheric balloon over Antarctica, drifting in the polar vortex at about 30-40 km altitude, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons and local magnetic fields.

BARREL-1M was an individual Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses stratospheric balloon payload flown during the 2013 Antarctic BARREL campaign. Drifting at near-space balloon altitudes over Antarctica, it measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons and local magnetic fields to study electron loss and magnetospheric wave-particle interactions.

The Pas is a fixed ground-based magnetometer station at The Pas, Manitoba, Canada, operating by the Canadian CANOPUS/CDAWeb era in the late 1980s. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric and magnetospheric studies, including auroral electrojets, substorms, ULF waves, and geomagnetic disturbances.

The Colville National Forest/Newport geomagnetic observatory in northeastern Washington, USA, is a fixed ground station operating since about 1966. It measures vector geomagnetic field variations for studies of ionospheric and magnetospheric current systems, geomagnetic storms, and space-weather disturbances; there are no orbital or vantage-point changes.

Barentsburg (IAGA code BBG) is a ground-based geomagnetic observatory at Barentsburg, Svalbard, operational by the 1990s and continuing in modern archives. It measures vector geomagnetic field variations in the high-latitude auroral/polar-cap region for studies of ionospheric currents, substorms, magnetic storms, and polar geospace disturbances.

C/NOFS (Communication/Navigation Outage Forecasting System) was a USAF/NASA equatorial ionosphere mission launched in 2008 and operated until reentry in 2015. It remained in a low-inclination (~13°), elliptical low-Earth orbit (initially about 400 x 850 km, gradually decaying), measuring plasma density/composition, ion drifts, neutral winds, electric fields, and scintillation-related irregularities.

ISEE 2 was an ESA spacecraft in the NASA/ESA International Sun-Earth Explorer program, launched in 1977 and operated until reentry in 1987. It remained in a highly elliptical geocentric orbit, flying near ISEE 1 with variable separation to study Earth’s magnetosphere, bow shock, magnetopause, upstream solar wind plasma, magnetic fields, waves, and energetic particles.

LANL-1994, a Los Alamos National Laboratory geosynchronous spacecraft operational from 1994 to 2007, observed Earth’s inner magnetosphere from near geostationary orbit; its orbit did not change. It supported space-weather and magnetospheric studies with instruments such as MPA and SOPA measuring thermal plasma, energetic particles, and radiation-belt populations.

Glyndon Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based magnetometer station near Glyndon, Minnesota, USA, operational no later than the CDAWeb archived data era; exact start and end dates are not confidently documented here. It measures local geomagnetic-field variations used for ionospheric, magnetospheric, ULF-wave, substorm, and space-weather studies.

Saint-Félicien Geophysical Observatory is a ground geomagnetic station at Saint-Félicien, Quebec, Canada, operating at least during the CDAWeb-era records to measure local magnetic-field variations with ground magnetometers for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and geomagnetic-activity studies; as a fixed ground site it has no orbital phases.

IMP-8 (Explorer 50; 1973-2001) was a NASA interplanetary monitor in a high-altitude geocentric orbit, often described as nearly circular at about 35 Earth radii with a ~12.5-day period, repeatedly sampling the upstream solar wind, bow shock/magnetosheath, and distant magnetotail. It measured magnetic fields, plasma, energetic particles, and cosmic rays for heliospheric and magnetospheric studies.

NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO, launched 2010) is a heliophysics mission in an inclined geosynchronous Earth orbit (near 102°W longitude, 24-hour period); its observing orbit has not changed over the mission. SDO provides near-continuous full-disk solar observations with AIA EUV/UV imaging, HMI magnetic/helioseismic measurements, and EVE solar EUV irradiance.

Pevek Geophysical Observatory (opened circa 1957) is a ground-based geomagnetic station at Pevek, Chukotka, Russia, operating high-latitude magnetometers to record geomagnetic field variations, auroral-zone disturbances, magnetic storms, and ionospheric/geospace current systems; it has no orbital phases.

Pine Ridge Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetic observatory at Pine Ridge, South Dakota, USA; its operational start and end years are not reliably specified in the SPASE/CDAWeb metadata I can confirm. It measures local geomagnetic-field variations with magnetometers for geospace, ionospheric-current, and space-weather studies; no orbit or relocation applies.

MMS-3 (launched 2015) is one of NASA’s four Magnetospheric Multiscale spacecraft, providing high-time-resolution fields, plasma, and energetic-particle data for magnetic reconnection, acceleration, and turbulence. It flew in a close tetrahedral formation in highly elliptical Earth orbit: 2015-early 2017 at about 1.2 x 12 RE for dayside magnetopause studies, then from 2017 onward after apogee raising to about 25 RE for magnetotail and broader magnetospheric campaigns.

BARREL-1G was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL high-altitude balloon payload that flew during the 2013 Antarctic campaign, drifting in the stratospheric circumpolar vortex rather than orbiting Earth. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer and GPS/ephemeris data, for conjugate studies with the Van Allen Probes.

THEMIS-E (Probe E/P4), launched in 2007, is one of NASA’s THEMIS substorm spacecraft. After 2007 commissioning and orbit placement, it has remained in a near-equatorial, highly elliptical geocentric orbit (inner THEMIS probe, about 1-day period with magnetospheric apogee), measuring electric and magnetic fields, plasma, and energetic particles in Earth’s plasma sheet and inner magnetosphere.

NOAA-6 was a NOAA polar-orbiting environmental satellite (launched 1979, operated until 1987) in a near-circular Sun-synchronous low Earth polar orbit at roughly 800–850 km altitude and ~99° inclination; its orbit did not have distinct science phases. Its Space Environment Monitor measured trapped and precipitating energetic electrons and protons for magnetospheric, radiation-belt, and space-weather studies.

The Boulder Magnetometer (IAGA code BOU) is a ground geomagnetic observatory near Boulder, Colorado, USA, operational since 1963. It has no orbital phases; it records continuous local vector geomagnetic field variations used to study ionospheric currents, geomagnetic storms, magnetospheric disturbances, and space-weather conditions.

NOAA-5 was a NOAA polar-orbiting environmental satellite launched in 1976 and operated until 1979. It remained in a near-polar, Sun-synchronous low-Earth orbit throughout its mission, with no distinct relocation phases. Its Solar Proton Monitor measured energetic proton and alpha-particle fluxes for space-weather and near-Earth particle-environment studies.

Ottawa (OTT) is a ground-based IAGA geomagnetic observatory in Ottawa, Ontario, Canada, operating since 1968. Its magnetometers record local vector geomagnetic field variations for studies of geomagnetic activity, magnetospheric currents, ionospheric disturbances, and space weather, and its data contribute to IAGA/INTERMAGNET-style global observatory networks.

Bettles Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground station at Bettles, Alaska, USA (no orbit; operational start and end are not reliably documented in this summary, but it appears in historical CDAWeb/SPASE high-latitude records). It measures local geomagnetic-field variations with ground magnetometers for auroral, ionospheric-current, and magnetospheric studies.

RBSP-A (Van Allen Probe A; launched 2012, science operations ended 2019) studied Earth’s Van Allen radiation belts and inner magnetosphere. Throughout the mission it flew a highly elliptical, low-inclination near-equatorial Earth orbit repeatedly sampling perigee-to-apogee regions through the belts; only end-of-mission perigee-lowering maneuvers occurred in 2019. Instruments measured fields, waves, energetic particles, and radiation.

BARREL-1H was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses stratospheric balloon payload, operated during the 2013 Antarctic long-duration balloon campaign. It drifted at ~30–40 km over Antarctica and the Southern Ocean, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays/gamma rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation with GPS and geospace context data.

BARREL-2P was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses payload, flown as a long-duration stratospheric balloon over Antarctica during the second BARREL campaign in 2014, ending the same year. It supported Van Allen Probes radiation-belt studies by measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating energetic electrons, with magnetometer and position data.

The Improved Solar Observing Optical Network (ISOON) was a ground-based full-disk H-alpha solar telescope at the USAF/Sacramento Peak site in Sunspot, New Mexico, operating roughly from 2000 to 2013. It provided high-cadence chromospheric images and movies for monitoring flares, filaments, active regions, and space-weather-related solar activity.

NASA’s Mars Science Laboratory/Curiosity (launched 2011) cruised from Earth to Mars in 2011-2012, during which RAD measured interplanetary radiation and energetic particles. Since landing in Gale Crater in August 2012 it has operated as a Mars surface rover, measuring geology, atmosphere, climate, habitability, and the surface radiation environment; ephemerides give its changing traverse location on Mars.

NOAA’s GOES-12 (GOES-M, launched 2001; operational 2003-2013) was a geostationary environmental satellite for solar and space-weather monitoring. After geostationary checkout/storage in 2001-2003, it served as GOES-East near 75°W from 2003 to May 2010, then relocated near 60°W for South America coverage until 2013. It carried SXI for full-disk soft-X-ray coronal imaging plus XRS/EPS space-environment sensors.

Anchorage is an IAGA ground geomagnetic observatory in Anchorage, Alaska, operational from at least the IGY era in 1957, measuring local magnetic-field variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies; it has no orbit or changing vantage point.

Nuuk Geophysical Observatory (Godthåb/GHB or NUK), operating since about 1976, is a ground geomagnetic station at Nuuk, Greenland, in the Greenland magnetometer network. It measures local vector geomagnetic-field variations for auroral, ionospheric, and magnetospheric studies; as a fixed ground observatory it has no orbital phases.

New Horizons (launched 2006) is a NASA Pluto-Kuiper Belt/heliophysics spacecraft on a solar-escape heliocentric trajectory. It cruised to and observed Jupiter during a 2007 gravity-assist flyby, encountered the Pluto system in July 2015, flew by Kuiper Belt object Arrokoth in January 2019, and continues outward through the Kuiper Belt/outer heliosphere. SWAP and PEPSSI measure solar wind, pickup ions, and energetic particles.

La Ronge Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetometer site at La Ronge, Saskatchewan, Canada; it has no orbit. Operational dates are not fully verified, but CDAWeb holdings include THEMIS-era data from about 2006 onward. It records geomagnetic field variations for auroral currents, substorms, ULF waves, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling studies.

AeroCube-6A (AC6-A), launched in 2014 and operated for science through 2017, was a CubeSat radiation-belt mission in near-polar low Earth orbit (~620–700 km altitude, ~98° inclination), with no major orbital-phase changes beyond orbital decay. It measured energetic electron/proton fluxes with a dosimeter to study radiation-belt precipitation and microbursts.

BARREL-1A was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload flown on a long-duration stratospheric balloon over Antarctica during the early-2013 campaign. It drifted with the polar vortex at about 35–40 km rather than orbiting Earth, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation and local magnetic fields in conjunction with Van Allen Probes.

Paamiut Geophysical Observatory is a ground station in Paamiut, southwest Greenland, operational since at least the CDAWeb data era and used for geomagnetic monitoring. It operates a magnetometer measuring local magnetic-field variations associated with ionospheric currents, auroral activity, and magnetospheric disturbances; as a fixed ground observatory, it has no orbital phases.

NOAA GOES-9 was launched in 1995 and supplied CDAWeb space-environment data during 1995-1998. It remained in geostationary Earth orbit, serving as GOES-West near 135°W after checkout, with longitude stationkeeping rather than a new orbital regime. It measured geomagnetic field variations and near-Earth energetic particles using its magnetometer and space environment monitors.

unique_missions.mission_name: Reuven Ramaty High Energy Solar Spectroscopic Imager
unique_missions.description: RHESSI (Reuven Ramaty High Energy Solar Spectroscopic Imager) was a NASA SMEX mission launched in 2002 and operated until 2018. It remained in low-Earth orbit throughout the mission, a roughly 600 km, 38° inclination orbit that gradually decayed. RHESSI used rotating modulation collimators and germanium detectors to image and spectroscopically measure solar-flare hard X-ray and gamma-ray emission.

Linares Geophysical Observatory is a ground geomagnetic station at Linares, Chile, with records reported from at least the IGY era (1957 onward, end date not confirmed). It measures geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for studies of Earth’s magnetic field, ionospheric/magnetospheric currents, geomagnetic storms, and space weather; it has no orbital phases.

Pinawa Geophysical Observatory (PIN), operating in Pinawa, Manitoba, Canada since 1968, is a ground magnetic observatory measuring geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies; it contributes data to INTERMAGNET/CANMOS and CDAWeb.

Stanford Geophysical Observatory is a ground geomagnetic station at Stanford University, California; its exact operational start/end year is not confirmed in the registry, but it is a fixed ground site with no orbital or vantage-point changes. It operates a fluxgate magnetometer measuring local geomagnetic-field variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, ULF-wave, and space-weather studies.

Helios 1 (Helios-A) was a German/NASA solar probe launched in 1974; it returned inner-heliosphere science data mainly until 1982. Its vantage point did not change: it remained in a highly eccentric heliocentric near-ecliptic orbit of about 0.31-0.98 AU, period ~190 days, measuring solar-wind plasma, magnetic fields, energetic particles, cosmic rays, dust, and radio/plasma waves.

NOAA’s GOES-17 (launched 2018, ended 2023) was a geostationary GOES-R series weather and space-environment satellite. It checked out near 89.5°W in 2018, served as GOES-West at 137.2°W from 2019 to Jan 2023, then drifted to on-orbit storage near 105°W before retirement. Heliophysics sensors included MAG, EXIS, SEISS, and SUVI for fields, particles, solar X-rays/EUV, and solar imaging.

PENGUIn-4 is a ground geophysical observatory in Antarctica in the PENGUIn network, operating from at least the 2000s, using a magnetometer to record geomagnetic field variations for studies of polar ionospheric currents, substorms, ULF waves, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling; it has no orbital phases.

ESA-JAXA’s BepiColombo (launched 2018) is a dual-spacecraft Mercury/heliophysics mission. During its 2018-2026 cruise it traverses the inner heliosphere using Earth, Venus, and multiple Mercury flybys, making solar-wind and planetary encounter measurements. After Mercury orbit insertion planned in 2026, ESA’s MPO and JAXA’s Mio will study Mercury, its magnetic field, magnetosphere, exosphere, surface, and solar-wind interaction.

NASA's Galileo spacecraft (launched 1989, ended 2003) measured magnetic fields, plasma, energetic particles, dust, and radio/plasma waves for Jupiter-system science. It followed a Venus-Earth-Earth gravity-assist cruise in 1989-95, with Venus, Earth, Gaspra, and Ida encounters and interplanetary measurements, then orbited Jupiter in highly elliptical moon-crossing orbits from Dec 1995 until Jupiter impact in Sep 2003.

OMNI is a NASA virtual observatory/data set, not a spacecraft, providing near-Earth solar wind and IMF observations from 1963 to present. It combines and intercalibrates measurements from many upstream/near-Earth spacecraft, including IMP, ISEE, Wind, ACE, and DSCOVR, and time-shifts them to Earth’s bow-shock nose for heliospheric and geospace studies.

ESA’s Cluster-Tango (C4, launched 2000; science operations 2001-2024) was one of four Cluster spacecraft in evolving, highly elliptical near-polar Earth orbit throughout the mission, with controlled inter-spacecraft separations. It measured magnetic/electric fields, waves, plasma, and energetic particles in the magnetosphere, cusps, magnetotail, magnetopause, bow shock, and solar wind.

Brorfelde (BFE) was an IAGA ground geomagnetic observatory at Brorfelde, Denmark, operated from 1978 until about 2011/2012. It recorded vector and scalar geomagnetic field variations for studies of ionospheric and magnetospheric currents, magnetic storms, secular variation, and global observatory indices; it had no orbital phases.

ISEE-3/ICE (International Sun-Earth Explorer 3, launched 1978; operations ended 1997) measured solar wind plasma, interplanetary magnetic fields, energetic particles, cosmic rays, and waves. It occupied a Sun-Earth L1 halo orbit in 1978-1982; after lunar flyby maneuvers in 1982-1983 it made distant geomagnetic-tail observations, then a Dec 1983 lunar swingby put it in heliocentric orbit for comet Giacobini-Zinner (1985), Halley-era, and heliospheric studies.

THEMIS-Ground CHBG is the Chibougamau, Quebec, Canada station in the THEMIS/UCLA ground-based observatory network, operating from the 2006-2007 auroral season. It hosts a white-light all-sky imager recording wide-field auroral emissions to study substorm onset and auroral dynamics, coordinated with THEMIS spacecraft observations.

Snap Lake Geophysical Observatory (operational by 2006; end date not identified) is a ground geomagnetic station near Snap Lake, Northwest Territories, Canada, represented in CDAWeb/THEMIS-GMAG holdings as SNKQ. It measures local magnetic-field variations for auroral, ionospheric, and magnetospheric studies; it has no orbital phases.

Rørvik Geophysical Observatory (IAGA RVK, operating since about 1985) is a fixed ground-based geomagnetic observatory at Rørvik, Norway, not a spacecraft. It records local vector geomagnetic field variations for studies of ionospheric currents, auroral electrojets, magnetic storms, substorms, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling; its observing location has not changed.

Fort Nelson Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground-based geomagnetic station at Fort Nelson, British Columbia, Canada, operating since at least the CDAWeb data era to measure local magnetic-field variations for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies; it has no orbital phases or changing space vantage point.

BARREL-1C was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload flown over Antarctica in 2013. It was a stratospheric long-duration balloon, not a spacecraft, drifting at high altitude over the Antarctic polar region to measure bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, plus magnetic-field/ULF-wave context for magnetospheric loss studies.

Whitehorse Geophysical Observatory (WHI), operating since 1957 in Whitehorse, Yukon, Canada, is a fixed ground magnetic observatory with no orbital phases. It measures geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for ionospheric, auroral, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies and contributes data to networks such as INTERMAGNET.

The Longyearbyen Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetometer station at Longyearbyen, Svalbard (78.2°N, 15.8°E), operational by 1991 in the IMAGE magnetometer network and used in CDAWeb. It measures high-latitude geomagnetic field variations, auroral electrojets, and cusp/polar-cap current systems; its location/vantage point does not change.

Uummannaq Geophysical Observatory (UMQ) is a ground geomagnetic station at Uummannaq, Greenland, operating since at least the 1970s as part of Greenland high-latitude magnetometer monitoring. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for auroral-zone ionospheric current, substorm, and magnetosphere studies; CDAWeb holdings may cover only selected years.

Cape Dorset Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground geomagnetic station at Cape Dorset/Kinngait, Nunavut, Canada, in operation since at least the early 1980s. It measures local geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for ionospheric, magnetospheric, auroral-zone, and space-weather studies; it has no orbital phases or changing vantage point.

NASA’s Parker Solar Probe (launched 2018) studies the solar corona, solar-wind origin, magnetic fields, plasma, energetic particles, and inner-heliospheric white-light structure. From 2018-2024 it used repeated Venus gravity assists to shrink a highly elliptical heliocentric orbit with progressively closer perihelia and some Venus-flyby science; from late 2024 onward it flies its final close solar orbit, reaching about 9.9 solar radii.

BARREL-2I was one payload in NASA’s BARREL Antarctic balloon array, flown in 2014 during the second BARREL campaign. It was a stratospheric circumpolar balloon over Antarctica/Southern Ocean, not an orbiting spacecraft, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation plus local magnetic fields to study magnetospheric loss processes.

Lyford Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground-based geomagnetic station at Lyford, Texas, USA, measuring local magnetic-field variations with a magnetometer for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies; it has no orbital phases or relocations. Operational start/end years are not confidently confirmed in available metadata.

San Juan WDC (IAGA code SJG) is a ground geomagnetic observatory in Puerto Rico, at/near San Juan and now near Cayey, operational since 1903. It measures local geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers, supporting studies of magnetic storms, Sq currents, and ionospheric/magnetospheric disturbances; data are distributed via the World Data Center/CDAWeb network.

Kevo Geophysical Observatory (KEV), in Kevo/Utsjoki, northern Finland, is a fixed ground station, not a spacecraft. Operating since the IGY-era and in the IMAGE magnetometer network from the early 1980s, it records geomagnetic field variations for auroral-zone ionospheric and magnetospheric studies.

BARREL-2O was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL stratospheric balloon payload flown during the second Antarctic campaign in 2013-2014, drifting in the Antarctic polar vortex at ~30-40 km altitude rather than orbiting Earth. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, with magnetic and GPS/trajectory context, to study radiation-belt loss.

Kapuskasing Geophysical Observatory (IAGA KAP), established in the late 1960s and still active, is a fixed ground magnetic observatory near Kapuskasing, Ontario, Canada. It has no orbital phases; it records geomagnetic field components and variations with magnetometers for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies, as part of Canada’s observatory network and INTERMAGNET.

FOXSI-2, the second Focusing Optics X-ray Solar Imager sounding-rocket flight, operated only on 2014-12-11 during a brief ballistic suborbital launch from White Sands Missile Range. It observed the Sun above the atmosphere with grazing-incidence focusing optics and hard X-ray detectors to image faint coronal X-ray emission related to flares, particle acceleration, and coronal heating.

unique_missions.mission_name: Département d'Astronomie Solaire de l'Observatoire de Paris, Paris, France
unique_missions.description: Observatoire de Paris’s Département d’Astronomie Solaire at Meudon, France, is a ground-based solar observatory, with spectroheliograph operations dating from 1909 and continuing in modern form. It records full-disk solar spectroheliograms in lines such as H-alpha, Ca II K, and Ca II 8542 for chromospheric/photospheric structure, filaments, plages, prominences, and solar activity studies.

Fort Yates Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetometer station at Fort Yates, North Dakota, USA, used for geomagnetic-field variation observations relevant to ionospheric and magnetospheric current systems and space-weather studies; it has no orbit or spacecraft phases.

TIMED (launched 2001) is a NASA heliophysics/upper-atmosphere mission in a near-circular low-Earth orbit, about 625 km altitude and 74° inclination; its orbit has had no major phase change. It studies the mesosphere, lower thermosphere, and ionosphere, measuring temperature, composition, winds, airglow, and solar EUV irradiance with instruments including SABER, GUVI, TIDI, and SEE.

BARREL-1I was a single NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses stratospheric balloon payload operated in the 2013 Antarctic long-duration balloon campaign. It drifted at high altitude over Antarctica/Southern Ocean rather than orbiting, carrying X-ray scintillator and magnetometer measurements of radiation-belt electron precipitation and magnetospheric coupling.

BARREL-2F was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses stratospheric balloon payload, launched and ended in 2014 during the second Antarctic campaign. It drifted over Antarctica rather than orbiting, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation and local magnetic field variations to study electron loss, often with Van Allen Probes context.

The Poker Flat magnetometer is a ground-based IAGA geomagnetic station at Poker Flat Research Range near Fairbanks, Alaska, operating at least since the 1970s in CDAWeb/IAGA records. It measures local vector geomagnetic-field variations for auroral, ionospheric-current, substorm, and magnetospheric studies; its observing location has not changed.

Kuujjuaq Geophysical Observatory, operated by NRCan/CANMOS in Kuujjuaq, Quebec, Canada, is a fixed ground geomagnetic observatory, operational since about 1981 and ongoing, measuring vector geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for auroral-zone, ionospheric current, magnetic storm, and magnetospheric studies; it has no orbital phases.

Yohkoh (Solar-A) was Japan’s ISAS solar X-ray observatory, launched in 1991; routine science ended after attitude-control loss in December 2001, and it reentered in 2005. It remained in a near-circular low Earth orbit (~600 km altitude, ~31° inclination) throughout its mission, observing solar flares, coronal heating, and high-energy plasma with SXT, HXT, BCS, and WBS.

Puvirnituq Geophysical Observatory (PBQ), operational since at least 1991 and still active, is a fixed ground magnetometer observatory at Puvirnituq, Nunavik, Quebec, Canada. It records geomagnetic field variations for auroral ionosphere and magnetospheric studies, with data distributed through INTERMAGNET/CDAWeb.

unique_missions.description: Bennington is a ground-based geomagnetic station in Bennington, Vermont, USA, used in the THEMIS/GMAG ground network. Operational in CDAWeb from about 2006 with no orbital phases, it measures local vector geomagnetic-field variations for studies of ionospheric currents, substorms, and magnetosphere–ionosphere coupling.

MMS-4 is one of NASA’s four Magnetospheric Multiscale spacecraft (launched 2015, operating), measuring 3-D plasma distributions, energetic particles, and electric/magnetic fields. It began in a near-equatorial highly elliptical Earth orbit with apogee near 12 Re for dayside magnetopause encounters in 2015-2016; in 2017 apogee was raised to about 25 Re for magnetotail science, with later extended phases sampling the magnetopause, bow shock, magnetosheath, and tail.

Derby Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground geomagnetic station at Derby, Western Australia, operational by the late 20th century in CDAWeb/space-physics archives; no orbit or relocation applies. Its magnetometers measure local geomagnetic field components and variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, geomagnetic-storm, and space-weather studies.

ESA’s PROBA2 (launched 2009) is a technology-demonstration microsatellite that has remained in low-Earth Sun-synchronous orbit. It supports solar and space-weather science, observing solar EUV coronal emission with SWAP and solar irradiance/flare variability with the LYRA radiometer, with additional in-situ plasma instruments for the near-Earth environment.

Ekati Geophysical Observatory (operational since about 1998) is a ground magnetic station at the Ekati diamond mine in Canada’s Northwest Territories. It measures geomagnetic field variations with fluxgate magnetometers for high-latitude magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling, auroral electrojet, and ionospheric current studies; its location/vantage point has not changed.

Tiksi Geophysical Observatory (IAGA TIK), established in 1957 at Tiksi, Sakha Republic, Russia, is a fixed high-latitude Arctic ground observatory, not a spacecraft. It records geomagnetic field variations with fluxgate/absolute magnetometers for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies; CDAWeb holdings contain available digital magnetometer intervals.

Kodiak Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetometer station on Kodiak Island, Alaska, active in heliophysics data archives at least from the late 20th century, measuring local geomagnetic-field variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, auroral, and space-weather studies; it has a fixed ground location and no orbital phases.

Baranov Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based high-Arctic geomagnetic station at or near Cape Baranova, Bolshevik Island, Severnaya Zemlya, Russia. It operated at least during the 1980s-1990s, using magnetometers to record local geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies.

BARREL-2A was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload launched over Antarctica in December 2013 and operated into January 2014. It was a long-duration stratospheric balloon, not an orbital spacecraft, drifting over Antarctica to measure bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetic field, GPS, and engineering data.

Carson City Geophysical Observatory was a fixed ground magnetic observatory in Carson City, Nevada, USA; authoritative start/end dates are not clear from the supplied registry. It operated magnetometers measuring local geomagnetic-field variations for geomagnetic, ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies, with no orbital or relocation phases.

unique_missions.mission_name: Rocket Experiment for Neutral Upwelling 2, RENU 2, Sounding Rocket Payload
unique_missions.description: RENU 2 (Rocket Experiment for Neutral Upwelling 2) was a NASA sounding-rocket payload launched from Andøya, Norway, in December 2015 and ended with that suborbital flight. It traversed the auroral/cusp ionosphere for minutes, measuring thermal plasma, electric and magnetic fields, waves, and auroral emissions to study neutral upwelling and ionospheric outflow.

Coral Harbour Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetometer station at Coral Harbour (Salliq), Southampton Island, Nunavut, Canada, operational in the space-physics data record from at least 1992. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for high-latitude auroral, ionospheric-current, and magnetospheric studies; there is no spacecraft orbit.

Geotail (JAXA/NASA, 1992-2022) studied Earth’s magnetotail, magnetosphere, bow shock, and solar wind with plasma, particle, electric- and magnetic-field instruments. From 1992 to late 1994 it used lunar swingbys to sample the distant magnetotail, reaching roughly 80-220 Earth radii downtail; from 1995 onward it remained in a lower highly elliptical geocentric orbit sampling the near-tail and dayside boundary regions.

Akulivik Geophysical Observatory (operational by 2006; no end date reported) is a fixed ground station at Akulivik, Nunavik, Quebec, Canada, not a spacecraft. It records high-latitude geomagnetic field variations, chiefly with fluxgate magnetometers, for studies of auroral ionospheric currents, substorms, ULF waves, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling in Canadian/CDAWeb data products.

DMSP F17 was a U.S. Defense Meteorological Satellite Program 5D-3 spacecraft (launched 2006, operated to 2022) for space-weather and environmental monitoring. It remained in a near-circular Sun-synchronous polar low-Earth orbit, about 840 km altitude and 98–99° inclination, measuring auroral particle precipitation, ionospheric plasma/drifts, magnetic fields, and near-Earth geospace conditions with instruments such as SSJ/5, SSIES, and SSM.

Remus Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetometer station at Remus, Michigan, USA, with CDAWeb records beginning around 2006 and no orbit or relocation. It measures local geomagnetic field vector variations for studies of magnetic storms, substorms, ULF waves, and space-weather coupling to Earth’s magnetosphere and ionosphere.

DSCOVR (Deep Space Climate Observatory, launched 2015) is a NOAA/NASA/USAF mission in a halo/Lissajous orbit about the Sun-Earth L1 point from mid-2015 onward; its orbit has not changed. For heliophysics it provides upstream solar wind plasma and interplanetary magnetic-field measurements for space-weather monitoring and studies, using the PlasMag instrument suite.

NOAA-12 (launched 1991, decommissioned 2007) was a NOAA POES polar weather satellite that remained in low-Earth, near-polar Sun-synchronous orbit throughout its mission. For heliophysics it carried the Space Environment Monitor, including TED and MEPED sensors, measuring precipitating/trapped energetic electrons and protons in Earth’s radiation belts, auroral zones, and near-Earth space environment.

FOXSI-1 (Focusing Optics X-ray Solar Imager flight 1) was a NASA sounding-rocket solar mission launched and completed on 2012-11-02 from White Sands Missile Range. It followed a single suborbital ballistic trajectory above Earth’s atmosphere, not an Earth orbit, providing minutes of solar pointing to demonstrate focusing hard-X-ray imaging spectroscopy of active regions and microflares.

FAST (Fast Auroral Snapshot Explorer) was a NASA SMEX mission launched in 1996 and operated until 2009 in a highly elliptical, near-polar low-Earth orbit (about 350 × 4175 km, 83° inclination) crossing the auroral zones. It measured auroral acceleration-region particles, electric and magnetic fields, plasma waves, and UV emissions for magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling studies.

BARREL-4H was a NASA/Dartmouth high-altitude Antarctic balloon payload in the BARREL radiation-belt campaign, operating during its 2016 flight over Antarctica. It drifted with polar stratospheric winds, carrying an X-ray spectrometer to measure bremsstrahlung from precipitating radiation-belt electrons and support Van Allen Probes magnetospheric loss studies.

STEREO-B (Behind), launched 2006, was NASA’s trailing Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory spacecraft. In late 2006–early 2007 it used highly elliptical Earth phasing orbits with lunar flybys, then entered a heliocentric orbit drifting behind Earth, observing solar eruptions and the heliosphere with SECCHI, IMPACT, PLASTIC, and S/WAVES until contact was lost in 2014.

Nurmijärvi (NUR) is a Finnish Meteorological Institute ground geomagnetic observatory in southern Finland (near 60.5°N, 24.7°E), operating since 1953. It has no orbit; it records continuous local vector magnetic-field variations, contributing to IAGA/INTERMAGNET and the IMAGE network for ionospheric, magnetospheric, auroral-electrojet, and space-weather studies.

BARREL-4C was one Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload, operated in 2016 as a high-altitude stratospheric balloon in the northern polar campaign launched from Esrange/Kiruna, Sweden, not a spacecraft orbit. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with GPS ephemeris and housekeeping, for magnetospheric space-weather studies.

Shumagin (SHU) is a USGS/IAGA ground geomagnetic observatory in the Shumagin Islands near Sand Point, Alaska, operational since about 2003. It has no orbit; it records local vector geomagnetic field variations for magnetospheric, ionospheric, auroral, and space-weather studies.

ChroTel (Chromospheric Telescope) is a ground-based robotic full-disk solar telescope at Observatorio del Teide, Tenerife, Spain, with routine synoptic operation from 2012 after 2008 commissioning. It images the solar chromosphere in H-alpha, Ca II K, and He I 10830 Å for studies of filaments, plages, coronal holes, and solar activity.

Upernavik Geophysical Observatory (UPN), a fixed ground station at Upernavik, northwest Greenland (~72.8°N, 56.1°W), has operated since at least the early 1980s as part of Greenland/high-latitude magnetometer networks. It records local geomagnetic field variations for auroral electrojet, ionospheric current, and magnetospheric disturbance studies; no orbital phases apply.

Shawano Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based fluxgate magnetometer station at Shawano, Wisconsin, USA, with CDAWeb data beginning in 2006 and no confirmed end year. It measures local three-component geomagnetic field variations and ULF perturbations for studies of ionospheric currents, substorms, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling; its observing location is fixed on the ground.

Nain Geophysical Observatory (operational by at least the 1980s; exact start/end not confirmed) is a fixed ground magnetometer/geophysical station at Nain, Labrador, Canada, measuring local geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies in high-latitude monitoring networks; it has no orbital phases.

BARREL-2W was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload flown in the 2013-2014 Antarctic campaign. It was a stratospheric balloon over Antarctica, not an orbiting spacecraft, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons and magnetic perturbations to study wave-particle interactions.

TWINS-2 (launched 2008 on a U.S. national-security host satellite) is a NASA Explorer Mission of Opportunity for magnetospheric remote sensing. It has remained in a 12-hour, high-inclination Molniya-type highly elliptical Earth orbit, imaging Earth’s ring current and magnetosphere with energetic neutral atom spectrometers and measuring geocoronal/interplanetary neutral H via a Lyman-alpha detector.

NASA’s Dawn spacecraft (2007-2018) was an ion-propelled planetary mission to the asteroid belt. After heliocentric cruise and a February 2009 Mars gravity-assist flyby, it orbited Vesta from July 2011 to September 2012, then transferred to Ceres, entering orbit in March 2015 and remaining in successive Ceres mapping orbits until mission end in 2018. It measured geology, topography, mineralogy, elemental composition, and ephemeris/trajectory.

BARREL-5A was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL stratospheric balloon payload operated during a single Antarctic long-duration balloon flight in the Van Allen Probes era (2013–2014 campaign period; exact flight dates should be verified). Flying at roughly 30–40 km over Antarctica, it measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation for magnetospheric loss studies.

Kullorsuaq Geophysical Observatory (operational by 1991; still active as far as IMAGE/CDAWeb records indicate) is a ground magnetometer station at Kullorsuaq, Greenland, in the high-latitude IMAGE magnetometer network, measuring geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric current, auroral, and magnetospheric studies.

SAMPEX (Solar, Anomalous, and Magnetospheric Particle Explorer, 1992-2012) flew a single decaying near-polar low-Earth orbit, initially about 520 x 670 km at 82° inclination, until atmospheric reentry. It measured energetic ions and electrons in near-Earth space, including anomalous cosmic rays, solar energetic particles, trapped radiation-belt and magnetospheric populations, using instruments such as HILT, MAST, PET, and LICA.

BARREL-4G was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload operated in the fourth Antarctic long-duration-balloon campaign (2015-2016). It drifted in the stratosphere over Antarctica, not in space orbit, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation to study magnetospheric wave-particle interactions and atmospheric loss.

Alouette 2 was a Canadian topside-sounder satellite launched in 1965 and operated until 1975. It remained in a near-polar, highly elliptical Earth orbit, about 500 km perigee, 3,000 km apogee, and 80° inclination, sounding the topside ionosphere and lower plasmasphere with radio instruments and in situ plasma measurements of electron density and ionospheric structure.

NOAA-7 (launched 1981; operated until 1986) was a NOAA TIROS-N-series polar weather satellite in low-Earth, near-polar Sun-synchronous orbit, with no major orbital phase changes. Its Space Environment Monitor measured energetic electron and proton fluxes, including trapped and precipitating particles, for radiation-belt, auroral, and space-weather studies.

BARREL-3D was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL stratospheric balloon payload flown in the 2015-2016 Antarctic campaign, drifting at high altitude over Antarctica rather than orbiting Earth. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with supporting magnetometer and ephemeris data, to study magnetospheric loss processes in conjunction with Van Allen Probes.

unique_missions.mission_name: Kanzelhöhe Solar Observatory, Karl-Franzens-Universität, Graz, Austria
unique_missions.description: Kanzelhöhe Solar Observatory (KSO), University of Graz, began regular solar patrol observations in 1944 from Kanzelhöhe near Villach, Austria (ground based, no orbit). It monitors solar activity with full-disk optical imaging of the photosphere and chromosphere, including white-light sunspots, H-alpha flares/filaments/prominences, and Ca II K plage/network; data are served through VSO.

Radisson Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetometer station at Radisson, Quebec, Canada, used in Canadian geospace monitoring and archived in CDAWeb. It measures geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric current and magnetospheric disturbance studies; there is no spacecraft orbit or changing vantage point. Operational start/end are not confidently verified here.

The College (CMO) geomagnetic observatory, operating since 1948 at the University of Alaska Fairbanks/College site near Fairbanks, Alaska, is a fixed ground station in the auroral zone. It measures continuous vector and scalar geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, auroral, and space-weather studies and contributes data to IAGA/INTERMAGNET.

MinXSS-1 (Miniature X-Ray Solar Spectrometer, launched to the ISS in 2015, deployed 2016, reentered 2017) was a 3U CubeSat solar irradiance mission. From May 2016 to May 2017 it operated in low Earth orbit after ISS deployment, measuring solar soft X-ray spectral irradiance with the X123 silicon drift detector for flares, active regions, and irradiance variability.

AeroCube-6B (AC6-B) was one of two Aerospace Corp./NSF CubeSats launched in 2014 into near-circular polar low Earth orbit, operating through 2017. It carried dosimeters to measure energetic electron/proton radiation in the inner magnetosphere and radiation belts, especially relativistic electron microbursts; its observing vantage remained LEO, with changing separation from AC6-A enabling two-point studies.

BARREL-4E was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload, operating as a long-duration high-altitude balloon over Antarctica during the 2016 BARREL campaign. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons for magnetospheric loss and space-weather studies, in conjunction with spacecraft such as the Van Allen Probes.

Global Oscillation Network Group (GONG, operational since 1995) is a six-site ground-based solar network at Big Bear, Cerro Tololo, El Teide, Learmonth, Mauna Loa, and Udaipur, providing near-continuous full-disk Doppler velocity, intensity/white-light, magnetogram, and later H-alpha observations for helioseismology and solar magnetic activity studies.

BARREL-3C was a Dartmouth/NASA BARREL stratospheric balloon payload, launched and operated in 2015 during the third BARREL campaign from Esrange/Kiruna, Sweden, flying at high altitude over northern high-latitude regions until flight termination that year. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays/gamma rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer and GPS context.

Ranua Geophysical Observatory (RAN), operating since at least the early 1980s, is a ground magnetometer station at Ranua, Finland in the IMAGE magnetometer network. It records geomagnetic field variations for studies of ionospheric currents, auroral electrojets, geomagnetic pulsations, and magnetospheric disturbances; it has no orbital phases.

NASA’s Pioneer 11 (launched 1973; last contact/mission end 1995) was a deep-space heliophysics and planetary probe. It cruised heliocentrically to Jupiter in 1973-74, flew through Jupiter’s magnetosphere in Dec 1974, traveled onward to Saturn in 1974-79, flew by Saturn in Sep 1979, then continued on a heliocentric escape trajectory measuring solar wind, magnetic fields, plasma, energetic particles, and cosmic rays.

Kilpisjärvi Geophysical Observatory (operational since about 1981) is a fixed ground observatory at Kilpisjärvi in Finnish Lapland, in the auroral zone. It supports heliophysics and space-weather studies with all-sky auroral optical imaging and geomagnetic field variation measurements; its KIL magnetometer station is part of the IMAGE network.

CLASP2 (Chromospheric LAyer SpectroPolarimeter 2) was a NASA/JAXA/NAOJ/European suborbital solar sounding-rocket experiment launched from White Sands in 2019 and ended after its brief flight. It did not enter orbit; it made minutes of above-atmosphere UV spectropolarimetric observations of the Sun’s lower atmosphere, measuring Mg II h/k and nearby lines plus slit-jaw context to infer chromospheric/photospheric magnetic fields.

Mauna Loa Solar Observatory (MLSO, operational since 1965) is a ground-based solar observatory on Mauna Loa, Hawaii, providing synoptic daytime observations of the solar chromosphere and low corona. It measures coronal white-light brightness/polarization and chromospheric/He I features for solar and heliospheric studies, with instruments including the Mk3/Mk4 and K-Cor coronagraphs.

DMSP 5D-3/F18 is a U.S. Defense Meteorological Satellite Program spacecraft launched in 2009 and operating in a near-circular, Sun-synchronous polar low-Earth orbit at about 830–850 km; its orbital class has not changed. It monitors space weather and the upper atmosphere/ionosphere, including auroral particle precipitation, thermal plasma, magnetic fields, and environmental imagery.

NASA’s Voyager 2 (launched 1977) is a planetary and heliospheric probe on a heliocentric escape trajectory. It flew by Jupiter in 1979, Saturn in 1981, Uranus in 1986, and Neptune in 1989, measuring planetary magnetospheres, plasma, fields, particles, and waves; afterward it explored the outer heliosphere, crossed the termination shock in 2007 and the heliopause in 2018, and now samples the very local interstellar medium.

Cluster-Rumba (Cluster 1/FM5) is one of ESA’s four Cluster II spacecraft, launched in 2000 and operated for science until 2024. It remained in a highly elliptical, near-polar Earth orbit throughout the mission, with evolving apogee/perigee geometry and variable formation separations, measuring fields, waves, plasma, and energetic particles in the magnetosphere, bow shock, magnetosheath, and solar wind.

PENGUIn-1 is an Antarctic ground magnetometer station in the Polar Experiment Network for Geospace Upper-atmosphere Investigations, operational from about 2010 with CDAWeb records in the 2010s. It has no orbit; it measures local geomagnetic-field variations for studies of auroral electrodynamics, ionospheric and magnetospheric current systems, ULF waves, and space weather.

BARREL-2T was a NASA Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses stratospheric balloon payload from the second Antarctic BARREL campaign, operating during its 2014 flight over Antarctica/Southern Ocean at roughly 30–40 km altitude. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer and GPS/ephemeris data supporting Van Allen Probes studies.

The Meanook Magnetometer (IAGA code MEA) is a ground geomagnetic observatory near Meanook/Athabasca, Alberta, Canada, operating since 1916. It has no orbit; fixed magnetometers measure the local vector magnetic field and its variations for studies of geomagnetic storms, magnetospheric/ionospheric currents, pulsations, and space weather.

NOAA’s GOES-15 (launched 2010; operated 2010-2020) was a geostationary environmental satellite. After checkout/storage near 90°W in 2010-2011, it served as GOES-West near 135°W from late 2011 to 2018, then operated in a supplemental/standby role near 128°W until decommissioning in 2020. MAG, EPS/HEPAD, SEM, and XRS measured magnetic fields, energetic particles, and solar X-rays.

Phobos 2 (USSR, launched 1988; contact lost March 1989) studied Mars, Phobos, and the solar-wind interaction with Mars with imaging, plasma/ion, magnetic-field, energetic-particle, and wave instruments. It cruised heliocentrically from Earth to Mars in 1988-Jan 1989, entered a highly elliptical Mars orbit in Jan-Feb 1989, then maneuvered in Feb-Mar 1989 into a near-equatorial, near-Phobos-synchronous Mars orbit for Phobos approach operations.

Homer Geophysical Observatory (HOM) is a fixed ground magnetometer station at Homer, Alaska, USA (about 59.6°N, 151.6°W). Documented in CDAWeb-era archives from 1978, it measures local geomagnetic-field variations for auroral, ionospheric, and magnetospheric current/substorm studies; as a ground site it has no orbital phases or changing vantage point.

BARREL-1D was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL stratospheric balloon payload flown during the 2013 Antarctic campaign, drifting at high altitude over Antarctica rather than orbiting Earth. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer data, to study substorms and wave-particle interactions in near-Earth space.

BARREL-4B was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL high-altitude balloon payload, launched and ended in 2016 during an Arctic stratospheric campaign from Esrange near Kiruna, Sweden, not an orbital spacecraft. It studied geospace radiation-belt electron precipitation by measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays with scintillator detectors, with GPS and ancillary field/housekeeping data for Van Allen Probes conjunctions.

BARREL-3A was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses payload, launched in Antarctica during the 2015-2016 campaign and ended in 2016.
