It was a long-duration stratospheric balloon, not an orbiting spacecraft, drifting circumpolarly at ~30-40 km altitude while measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer and GPS/ephemeris support.

BARREL-1R was an individual NASA/Dartmouth BARREL high-altitude balloon payload operated in the 2013 Antarctic campaign. It drifted in the Antarctic stratosphere, not in orbit, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation and related magnetospheric activity, with magnetometer, GPS, and engineering data.

Nord (IAGA code NRD) is a ground-based geomagnetic observatory at Station Nord in northeast Greenland, operational since at least the 1990s. It measures local vector magnetic-field variations for studies of polar ionospheric currents, auroral electrojets, magnetic storms, and magnetosphere–ionosphere coupling, and contributes to IAGA/INTERMAGNET-style geomagnetic networks.

Red Deer Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetometer site at Red Deer, Alberta, Canada, used for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies by measuring local geomagnetic field variations. It is associated with Canadian ground magnetic networks and CDAWeb holdings; its observing site/vantage is fixed, not orbital.

Eagle Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetic observatory at Eagle, Alaska, active in USGS/CDAWeb geomagnetic records but with operational start/end dates not confirmed here. It measures local geomagnetic field variations, typically with fluxgate magnetometers, for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies; no orbital phases apply.

BARREL-2L was one payload of NASA’s Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses, operated during the second Antarctic balloon campaign in 2013-2014. It was a stratospheric long-duration balloon launched from Antarctica and drifting in the southern polar vortex, carrying X-ray/gamma-ray and magnetic-field instruments to measure radiation-belt electron precipitation and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling.

SUNRISE2 was the second flight of the SUNRISE balloon-borne solar observatory, operating June 12-17, 2013. Launched from Esrange near Kiruna, Sweden, it flew at stratospheric altitude across the Arctic/Atlantic to northern Canada, observing the solar photosphere and chromosphere with high-resolution UV/visible imaging and magnetography, notably SuFI and IMaX.

LANL-1989 (launched 1989, operated to 2007) was a Los Alamos National Laboratory geosynchronous Earth-orbit spacecraft for magnetospheric and space-weather research. It stayed at/near GEO throughout its mission, sampling the near-Earth plasma sheet/ring-current region; MPA measured 3D ions/electrons and SOPA measured energetic particles.

BARREL-2M was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL high-altitude balloon payload operated in the 2013-2014 Antarctic campaign, drifting in the stratospheric polar vortex over Antarctica rather than orbiting Earth. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, with magnetometer and GPS data, to study electron loss and magnetosphere–ionosphere coupling.

Priddis Geophysical Observatory, operating since 1981 near Priddis, Alberta, Canada, is a ground geophysical site for heliophysics and space-weather studies. It measures local geomagnetic field variations with ground magnetometers, supporting ionospheric current, auroral, and magnetospheric disturbance studies; as a fixed ground observatory it has no orbital phases.

Hawkeye 1 (launched 1974, operated until 1978) was a University of Iowa/NASA heliophysics spacecraft in a highly elliptical near-polar Earth orbit, about 465 km perigee and 125,000 km apogee, not a low-altitude-only orbit. It measured high-latitude magnetospheric and ionospheric electrodynamics, auroral currents, magnetic fields, plasma waves/VLF emissions, and particle-related phenomena.

unique_missions.mission_name: Osservatorio Astrofisico di Catania, Via S.Sofia 78, 95123 Catania ITALY
unique_missions.description: INAF–Osservatorio Astrofisico di Catania (OACT), a ground-based observatory in Catania, Sicily, Italy, has carried out solar observations since the late 19th century (founded 1880). Its VSO solar data are optical full-disk photospheric continuum/white-light and Hα chromospheric images used to monitor sunspots, plages, filaments, flares, and other solar activity.

PENGUIn-3 is a ground geophysical observatory in Antarctica, part of the PENGUIn high-latitude geospace network, operational by the 2007–2008 IPY era. It uses ground magnetometers to record geomagnetic field variations for studies of polar ionospheric currents, auroral electrodynamics, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling; it has no orbit or moving vantage point.

NASA’s ICON (Ionospheric Connection Explorer; launched 2019) studied ionosphere-thermosphere coupling from a low-inclination (~27°), ~575 km low-Earth orbit that did not undergo major mission-phase changes. Science operations ran from late 2019 until contact was lost in Nov 2022 (mission formally ended 2024), using MIGHTI, FUV, EUV, and IVM for winds, airglow/UV emissions, and in situ plasma.

SuperDARN (Super Dual Auroral Radar Network) is an international ground-based HF coherent-scatter radar network, begun with Goose Bay in 1983 and organized/expanded as SuperDARN from 1995, with high- and mid-latitude radars in both hemispheres. It measures ionospheric plasma convection, electric fields, and decameter irregularities for magnetosphere–ionosphere coupling and space-weather studies.

The Barrow (BRW) geomagnetic observatory, operational since about 1949 at Barrow/Utqiaġvik, Alaska, is a ground-based high-latitude magnetometer station. It records local vector geomagnetic field variations for studies of auroral-zone ionospheric currents, magnetospheric disturbances, substorms, and space-weather activity, as part of the IAGA/INTERMAGNET-style observatory network.

Ukiah Geophysical Observatory (UKI) was a fixed ground geomagnetic observatory at Ukiah, California, USA, operating roughly 1931/1932 to about 1983. It recorded local geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers/variometers for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies; as a ground site it had no orbital phases.

Helios 2 (Helios-B) was a West German/NASA solar probe launched in 1976 and operated until 1980. It remained throughout the mission in a highly elliptical, near-ecliptic heliocentric orbit from about 0.29 AU perihelion to near 1 AU aphelion, measuring inner-heliospheric solar wind plasma, magnetic fields, energetic particles, radio/plasma waves, and dust.

Hopen Geophysical Observatory (IAGA HOP) is a fixed ground geomagnetic station on Hopen Island, Svalbard, operational by the late 20th century and used in CDAWeb data sets for high-latitude geomagnetic and ionospheric studies. It measures local geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers; there is no orbital or relocation history.

Lethbridge Geophysical Observatory (LTH; operating since 1986) is a ground magnetometer station at Lethbridge, Alberta, Canada, used in Canadian auroral/geospace networks including CANOPUS and successor CARISMA. It measures local geomagnetic field variations to study ionospheric currents, auroral activity, magnetic storms, ULF waves, and magnetospheric dynamics.

Kitt Peak Vacuum Tower Telescope (KPVT) was a ground-based full-disk solar observatory on Kitt Peak, Arizona, operated for synoptic solar magnetism from 1973 to 2003. It used the 512-channel magnetograph (to 1992) and later the spectromagnetograph (1992-2003) to measure photospheric line-of-sight magnetic fields, velocities, and related solar properties.

Fort Yukon Magnetometer is a ground geomagnetic observatory at Fort Yukon, Alaska (IAGA code FYU), operating at least from the 1970s into the late 1980s, measuring vector geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies in the high-latitude Alaska sector; it is part of IAGA/CDAWeb ground magnetometer holdings.

ST5-094 was one of NASA’s three Space Technology 5 microsatellites (launched and operated in 2006) in highly elliptical, near-polar low Earth orbit, about 300–4500 km altitude. It demonstrated miniaturized spacecraft technologies and carried a magnetometer to sample Earth’s magnetosphere/auroral regions; its orbit did not have later mission phases.

Loysburg Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground-based magnetometer station at Loysburg, Pennsylvania, USA, operational at least from 2000 in CDAWeb/MEASURE-era holdings; its end date is not confidently documented. It records local geomagnetic field variations for studies of magnetospheric currents, geomagnetic storms/substorms, and space weather, with no orbital or relocation phases.

NOAA-14 (NOAA-J, launched 1994; operational environmental service to 2005) was a NOAA polar-orbiting weather satellite in a near-polar, sun-synchronous low Earth orbit for its mission, with no major relocation. Its Space Environment Monitor measured energetic protons and electrons in near-Earth radiation belts and auroral/precipitating particle regions for magnetospheric and space-weather studies.

BARREL-1N was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses stratospheric balloon payload flown in the 2012-2013 Antarctic BARREL campaign. Drifting at roughly 30-40 km over Antarctica, it measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation and local magnetic/ULF wave signatures in conjunction with the Van Allen Probes.

The International Space Station, assembled in low Earth orbit beginning in 1998 and continuously crewed since 2000, is a 51.6°-inclination platform at roughly 330-420 km altitude; its orbit is periodically reboosted but has not changed regime. It supports heliophysics and space-environment measurements of ionospheric plasma, radiation, cosmic rays, and spacecraft charging with instruments such as AMS-02, FPMU, and TEPC.

Laurel Geophysical Observatory (operational start not confirmed; CDAWeb holdings document 20th-century use) is a ground-based geomagnetic station in Laurel, Maryland, USA. It operates magnetometers measuring local Earth magnetic-field variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, geomagnetic-storm, and pulsation studies; it has no orbital phases.

Suisei (PLANET-A) was an ISAS/Japan comet and solar-wind probe (launched 1985; operations ended 1992). It entered a low-inclination heliocentric orbit, imaged Comet Halley’s H I Lyman-alpha coma and measured solar-wind plasma, made a close Halley flyby on 8 Mar 1986 (~151,000 km), then continued heliocentric cruise with trajectory corrections toward an Earth-return flyby in Aug 1992.

Toolik Lake Geophysical Observatory (operational since at least the mid-1990s) is a fixed ground magnetometer station at Toolik Lake, Alaska, measuring geomagnetic field variations for high-latitude ionospheric and magnetospheric studies, including auroral currents, substorms, and ULF pulsations; its observing location does not change.

ISIS 1 (International Satellites for Ionospheric Studies; launched 1969, operated until 1984) was a Canadian/NASA ionospheric satellite in a highly inclined eccentric low-Earth orbit (~578 x 3526 km, ~88°). Its orbit had no planned relocation; it sampled the topside ionosphere and inner plasmasphere with a swept-frequency topside sounder, VLF/ELF receivers, and plasma/particle instruments.

ISIS 2 (International Satellites for Ionospheric Studies) was a Canadian/NASA topside-ionosphere satellite launched in 1971 and operated until 1990. It remained in a near-circular, near-polar low Earth orbit at about 1,350–1,420 km altitude and 88° inclination. It measured ionospheric electron density, plasma waves, particles, and auroral emissions; its SFS swept-frequency sounder produced topside ionograms.

THEMIS-B, renamed ARTEMIS P1, is a NASA probe launched in 2007 to measure magnetospheric/substorm plasma, fields, waves, and particles. It flew highly elliptical Earth orbits for THEMIS magnetotail science from 2007-2009, then used lunar-transfer trajectories in 2009-2010, operated near the Earth-Moon L2/L1 regions in 2010-2011, and entered lunar orbit in 2011, where it continues lunar/solar-wind plasma and fields observations.

SESAME (operational from 1988, with archived campaigns mainly in the late 1980s–1990s) was a Scandinavian auroral-zone ground observatory network in northern Fennoscandia, not a spacecraft. It measured ionospheric and magnetospheric variability using riometers, VLF/ELF receivers, all-sky imagers, Fabry–Perot interferometers, and magnetometers for auroral and space-weather studies.

NOAA-8 was a NOAA polar-orbiting environmental satellite launched in 1983 and operated until 1985. It remained in a near-circular, Sun-synchronous, near-polar low Earth orbit throughout the mission, carrying the Space Environment Monitor (SEM) to measure precipitating/trapped energetic electrons and protons for space-weather, radiation-belt, and auroral studies.

NASA/ESA/ASI Cassini (launched 1997, ended 2017) studied Saturn’s system and fields/particles. It cruised heliocentrically with gravity assists at Venus (1998, 1999), Earth (1999), and Jupiter (2000, with Jovian magnetosphere science), then entered Saturn orbit in 2004 for tour/extended missions through 2017, including 2017 ring-grazing/Grand Finale proximal orbits. MAG measured in-situ magnetic fields in the solar wind and planetary magnetospheres.

unique_missions.mission_name: NASA Stennis Space Center Geophysical Observatory
unique_missions.description: NASA’s Stennis Space Center Geophysical Observatory (IAGA BSL) is a ground geomagnetic station at Stennis/Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, USA, operating since about 1986 and still active. It is not in orbit; it records local vector geomagnetic-field variations with fluxgate magnetometers for geophysics, magnetospheric studies, and space-weather monitoring.

Richardson Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based magnetometer site in Richardson, Alaska; its exact operational start/end are not clear from SPASE/CDAWeb metadata. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, auroral, and space-weather studies, providing fixed high-latitude ground magnetic observations rather than any orbital vantage point.

Muono Geophysical Observatory (MUO) is a ground magnetometer station at Muonio, Finnish Lapland, operating in the IMAGE magnetometer network since at least the 1980s. It records local geomagnetic field variations used to study high-latitude ionospheric currents, auroral activity, geomagnetic storms, and substorms; it has no orbital phases.

ESA’s Giotto spacecraft (1985-1992) was a heliophysics/comet mission measuring cometary gas, dust, plasma, magnetic fields, and solar-wind interaction. Launched in 1985 into heliocentric cruise, it flew through Comet Halley’s coma in March 1986, hibernated in solar orbit, used an Earth gravity assist in July 1990, then encountered Comet Grigg-Skjellerup in July 1992 before operations ended.

Fredericksburg (FRD) is a USGS/IAGA ground geomagnetic observatory near Fredericksburg/Corbin, Virginia, USA, operating since 1956. It continuously records local vector magnetic-field variations and absolute geomagnetic measurements for geomagnetic storms, quiet-time variations, and space-weather studies; as a fixed ground station, it has no orbital phases.

MetOp-A was a EUMETSAT/ESA polar-orbiting meteorological satellite launched in 2006 and retired in 2021. During its science operations it flew a near-polar, Sun-synchronous low Earth orbit at about 817 km altitude with a mid-morning local time node; it was lowered/passivated for disposal in 2021. Its SEM-2 instrument measured energetic electrons, protons, and radiation-belt particle fluxes for space-weather and near-Earth magnetospheric studies.

NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft (launched 1977; operating) is a planetary/heliospheric probe. It flew by Jupiter in March 1979 and Saturn/Titan in November 1980 with fields, particles, plasma-wave, and remote-sensing observations, then followed a solar-system escape heliocentric trajectory north of the ecliptic. It crossed the termination shock in 2004 and heliopause in 2012, measuring energetic particles, magnetic fields, and plasma waves in the outer heliosphere and local interstellar medium.

Fort Simpson is a fixed ground-based IAGA magnetometer observatory at Fort Simpson, Northwest Territories, Canada, operational by about 1973 (exact start/end not verified here). It measures local geomagnetic-field variations for auroral electrojet, substorm, magnetic-storm, and high-latitude disturbance studies; it has no orbital phases.

ST5-155 was one of NASA’s three Space Technology 5 microsatellites, launched in 2006 and operated until mid-2006. It flew a highly elliptical, high-inclination low-Earth orbit, roughly 300–4500 km altitude at about 105.6° inclination, with no major orbital relocation. ST5 demonstrated miniature spacecraft technologies and measured Earth’s magnetic field for magnetospheric/space-weather studies.

LANL-1991 was a Los Alamos National Laboratory geosynchronous spacecraft launched in 1991 and operated through 2008, monitoring the near-Earth magnetosphere from GEO for its full mission. Its MPA and SOPA particle instruments measured magnetospheric plasma and energetic electron/ion fluxes, widely used for radiation-belt, substorm, and space-weather studies.

Daneborg Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetic station at Daneborg in northeast Greenland, operational in space-physics data sets since at least the early 1980s and still active. It measures geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for high-latitude ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies, and is included in the IMAGE/Greenland magnetometer networks.

NOAA’s GOES-6 satellite (1983-1994) was a geostationary Earth-orbiting observatory, repositioned among operational GOES longitudes but remaining near GEO throughout its mission. It monitored space weather at ~6.6 Earth radii with magnetometer and energetic-particle sensors measuring the geomagnetic field and magnetospheric particle environment.

BARREL-4D was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses stratospheric balloon payload, launched and operated in 2016 during BARREL's fourth campaign from Esrange near Kiruna, Sweden. Floating at ~30-40 km over the Arctic/subauroral region, it measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons for radiation-belt loss and magnetosphere-ionosphere studies.

BARREL-3B was a NASA/Dartmouth long-duration balloon payload in the BARREL program, launched for the 2013-2014 Antarctic campaign and ending after that single flight. It flew in the high-latitude stratosphere over Antarctica on circumpolar winds, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, with GPS/ephemeris and magnetic-field context for geospace studies.

Val-d'Or Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetic station at Val-d'Or, Quebec, Canada; its exact operational start/end are not confidently established here. It records local geomagnetic field variations with ground magnetometers for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and geomagnetic disturbance studies, with no orbital or vantage-point changes.

Schefferville Geophysical Observatory is a ground geophysical/magnetic station at Schefferville, Quebec, Canada, operational from the IGY era (about 1957) in high-latitude North America. It measures geomagnetic field variations with ground magnetometers for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies; as a fixed ground site it has no orbital phases.

Andenes Geophysical Observatory is a ground station at Andenes, northern Norway (about 69.3°N, 16.0°E), operational since at least the 1990s. It operates fluxgate magnetometers measuring local geomagnetic field variations as part of the IMAGE high-latitude magnetometer network, supporting ionospheric, magnetospheric, and auroral studies; it has no orbital phases.

MMS-2 is one of NASA’s four Magnetospheric Multiscale spacecraft, launched in 2015 to study magnetic reconnection, turbulence, and particle acceleration with high-rate plasma, fields, and energetic-particle instruments. In 2015-2016 it flew a highly elliptical Earth orbit of about 1.2 x 12 RE targeting the dayside magnetopause; in 2017 its apogee was raised to about 25 RE for magnetotail campaigns, continuing in this high-apogee geocentric orbit.

BARREL-4A was an individual NASA/Dartmouth BARREL stratospheric balloon payload, operated only during its 2016 Sweden/Arctic flight after launch from Esrange near Kiruna. It drifted at balloon altitude through the polar atmosphere, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays/gamma rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation for Van Allen Probes conjunction and magnetospheric loss studies.

Pic-du-Midi Observatory (OMP), founded in 1882, is a ground-based high-altitude solar observatory on Pic du Midi de Bigorre in the French Pyrenees, France. Its modern CLIMSO solar patrol has operated since 2007, imaging the solar disk, prominences, and low corona in white light and selected chromospheric/coronal lines such as H-alpha and Ca II for solar activity studies.

BARREL-2X was an individual NASA Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload flown on an Antarctic long-duration balloon during the second BARREL campaign in austral summer 2013-2014. From the stratosphere over/around Antarctica, it measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, magnetic field, and GPS position; it had no space orbit.

NOAA’s GOES-13 (launched 2006; NOAA operational 2010-2017) was a geostationary Earth/space-weather satellite. After checkout and on-orbit storage near 105°W in 2006-2010, it served as GOES-East near 75°W from 2010 to Dec 2017, measuring geosynchronous energetic particles, magnetic field, solar X-rays/EUV, and Earth weather imagery.

AMPTE-CCE (Charge Composition Explorer), launched in 1984 and operated until 1989, was one of the three AMPTE spacecraft. It remained in a near-equatorial, highly elliptical Earth orbit (about 1,100–50,000 km altitude) throughout the mission, sampling the inner magnetosphere, ring current, and radiation belts with energetic-particle, ion-composition, plasma, and fields measurements.

BARREL-2K was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses long-duration stratospheric balloon payload, launched and ended in 2014 during the Antarctic campaign. It drifted at balloon altitude over Antarctica rather than orbiting, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, with magnetometer and GPS context.

ELFIN-A (Electron Losses and Fields Investigation; launched 2018) is a UCLA 3U CubeSat in near-polar low Earth orbit, initially about 450 km altitude and ~93° inclination, with no major orbit changes aside from natural orbital decay. It measures radiation-belt electron and ion pitch-angle distributions plus magnetic fields to study wave-particle scattering and atmospheric precipitation.

Prince George Geophysical Observatory (PGEO) is a fixed ground geophysical/magnetic observatory at Prince George, British Columbia, Canada, operational at least during the THEMIS/CDAWeb era beginning in 2007. It has no orbital phases; it measures local geomagnetic-field variations with a ground magnetometer for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies.

The Mees CCD Imaging Spectrograph (MCCD), operating circa 1992–2009 at the University of Hawaii’s Mees Solar Observatory on Haleakala, Maui, was a ground-based solar imaging spectrograph. It observed from a fixed terrestrial site, recording CCD chromospheric and photospheric spectral line profiles for studies of active regions, flares, and the solar atmosphere.

NASA's MESSENGER (2004-2015) studied Mercury's surface, exosphere, magnetic field, magnetosphere, and solar-wind interaction. It cruised in heliocentric orbit from 2004-2011, with Earth (2005), Venus (2006, 2007), and Mercury flybys (2008, 2008, 2009) returning science, then orbited Mercury in a highly eccentric near-polar orbit from March 2011 until impact in April 2015.

Salluit Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetic station at Salluit, Nunavik, Quebec, Canada; the registry/data-system records do not give a confidently verified operational start or end year. It uses a fluxgate magnetometer to record geomagnetic field variations for high-latitude ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies, and has no orbital phases.

NASA’s Solar Maximum Mission (SMM, 1980-1989) was a Sun-pointed observatory in low Earth orbit for solar-flare, coronal, and irradiance studies. It remained in LEO throughout; after an attitude-control failure in 1980 it operated in a degraded mode until Shuttle repair and redeployment in 1984. Instruments included the Coronagraph/Polarimeter, hard X-ray and gamma-ray spectrometers, and irradiance monitors.

ACE (Advanced Composition Explorer, launched 1997) is a heliophysics and space-weather mission measuring upstream solar wind plasma, magnetic field, ion and isotope composition, and energetic particles. After launch and transfer, it entered a halo/Lissajous orbit about the Sun-Earth L1 point in 1997 and has remained there; flagship instruments include MAG, SWEPAM, SWICS, ACE-EPAM, SIS, and CRIS.

Dededo Geophysical Observatory (Guam; operational since about 1957 and active in modern CDAWeb/INTERMAGNET-era holdings) is a fixed ground magnetic observatory, not a spacecraft. It measures local geomagnetic field vector/intensity variations with magnetometers for ionospheric, magnetospheric, geomagnetic storm, and space-weather studies.

Cluster-Samba (ESA Cluster II spacecraft 3, launched 2000; science operations ended 2024) flew with the four-spacecraft Cluster constellation in highly elliptical, near-polar Earth orbits throughout the mission, with inter-spacecraft separations varied for campaigns. It measured Earth’s magnetosphere, bow shock, magnetopause, aurora, plasma, fields, waves, and energetic particles using instruments such as FGM, CIS, PEACE, EFW, STAFF, WHISPER, and RAPID.

Student Nitric Oxide Explorer (SNOE, 1998-2003) was a small NASA/STEDI low-Earth-orbit satellite in a near-circular, near-polar Sun-synchronous orbit about 535-580 km altitude until orbital decay/reentry. It studied the lower thermosphere and ionosphere, measuring nitric oxide ultraviolet airglow, solar soft X-rays, and auroral electrons/photons driving space-weather variability.

Dombås (DOB) is a ground geomagnetic observatory at Dombås, Norway, operational since at least the 1980s with CDAWeb/IMAGE digital coverage mainly from the 1990s onward. It measures local three-component magnetic field variations for studies of ionospheric currents, auroral electrojets, geomagnetic storms, and high-latitude magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling.

BARREL-3F was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses stratospheric balloon payload, launched and ended in 2015 during BARREL’s third campaign, apparently from Esrange/Kiruna, Sweden, drifting at stratospheric altitude over Arctic longitudes rather than orbiting. It measured X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, magnetic field, and ephemeris/housekeeping data.

Vostok (IAGA code VOS) is a ground geomagnetic observatory at Russia’s Vostok Station in inland East Antarctica (near 78.5°S, 106.9°E), operating from the International Geophysical Year era around 1957–1958 and continuing with possible data gaps. It records geomagnetic field variations for high-latitude ionospheric and magnetospheric studies; as a fixed ground station it has no orbital phases.

Apollo 12 Lunar Module/ALSEP (launched and deployed in November 1969; ALSEP operated until September 1977) was not an orbital spacecraft but a fixed lunar-surface station at the Oceanus Procellarum landing site. It measured the local lunar plasma, magnetic, seismic, and thermal environment; the Solar Wind Spectrometer and related plasma instruments observed solar wind ions/electrons from the Moon.

Kenai Geophysical Observatory is a ground geomagnetic station at Kenai, Alaska, in the USGS geomagnetic observatory network; it has no orbit or changing vantage point. Its operational start year/end status are not confirmed here. The station’s magnetometer measures local geomagnetic-field variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, auroral-current, and space-weather studies.

IBEX (Interstellar Boundary Explorer), launched in 2008, is a NASA heliophysics mission using IBEX-Lo and IBEX-Hi energetic-neutral-atom imagers to map the heliosphere’s outer boundary and solar-wind interaction with the local interstellar medium. It has remained in Earth orbit: 2008-2011 in a very high, highly elliptical orbit, then from 2011 in a more stable lunar-resonant high elliptical geocentric orbit.

Hov Faroe Islands Geophysical Observatory (IAGA HOV; operating since 1983, ongoing) is a fixed ground geomagnetic observatory near Hov on Suðuroy, Faroe Islands. It measures Earth’s local magnetic field and variations with magnetometers for ionospheric current, auroral/electrojet, geomagnetic storm, and space-weather studies; no orbital phases apply.

Apollo 15 Lunar Module/ALSEP (launched and deployed on the Moon in 1971; ALSEP operated until 1977) was a stationary lunar-surface observatory at the Hadley–Apennine landing site. It studied lunar geophysics and the near-surface plasma environment; the Solar Wind Spectrometer measured directional solar-wind proton and electron fluxes at the Moon.

The Inuvik (INK) Magnetic Observatory is a ground-based IAGA/INTERMAGNET geomagnetic station near Inuvik, Northwest Territories, Canada, operating since 1957. It continuously measures Earth’s magnetic field components and total intensity, supporting auroral-zone ionospheric, magnetospheric, geomagnetic-disturbance, and space-weather studies.

NOAA-16 (launched 2000, operated until 2014) was a POES satellite in a near-circular, Sun-synchronous polar low-Earth orbit (~850 km, ~99° inclination) throughout its mission. It carried SEM-2 instruments including MEPED and TED to measure trapped and precipitating energetic electrons/protons and auroral particles for space weather, radiation belt, and auroral studies.

Gjoa Haven Geophysical Observatory (GDH), operating since about 1968 at Gjoa Haven, Nunavut, Canada, is a fixed ground geomagnetic station. It measures vector magnetic-field variations for high-latitude ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies, as part of Canada’s geomagnetic observatory network and contributing INTERMAGNET/CDAWeb data.

Cambridge Bay Magnetometer (IAGA CBB) is a fixed ground geomagnetic observatory at Cambridge Bay, Nunavut, Canada, operational since the early 1970s. It measures local magnetic-field variations for studies of auroral electrojets, ionospheric/magnetospheric currents, and geomagnetic disturbances; its location has not changed.

Kangerlussuaq Geophysical Observatory, at Kangerlussuaq/Søndre Strømfjord in western Greenland (about 67°N, 51°W), is a ground high-latitude observatory operational since at least 1977. Its magnetometers measure local geomagnetic-field variations for studies of auroral ionospheric currents, substorms, and magnetospheric dynamics; it has no orbit.

CRRES (Combined Release and Radiation Effects Satellite) was a U.S. Air Force/NASA mission launched in 1990 and operated until failure in 1991. It remained in a highly elliptical geocentric transfer orbit, about 350 x 33,500 km at ~18° inclination, sampling the inner magnetosphere and radiation belts with particle, field, wave, and radiation-effects instruments, and conducting active chemical-release experiments.

Hot Springs Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetic observatory at Hot Springs, South Dakota, USA, operational from at least 1960 in available geomagnetic records. It uses ground magnetometers to measure local geomagnetic-field variations for studies of magnetic storms, ionospheric currents, and secular/space-weather geomagnetic activity; it has no orbital phases.

Savissivik Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetometer station at Savissivik, northwest Greenland, operational since at least the 1990s in CDAWeb records. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for high-latitude ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies; as a fixed ground site, it has no orbital phases.

GOES-10 (NOAA; launched 1997, operational 1998-2009) was a geostationary Earth weather and space-environment satellite. It served at about 135°W as GOES-West from 1998 to 2006, then was relocated to about 60°W from 2006 until retirement in 2009. Its SEM package measured magnetic fields, energetic particles, and solar X-rays for magnetospheric and space-weather studies.

NOAA-18 (NOAA-N), launched in 2005 and operational until 2025, was a NOAA POES satellite in a near-polar Sun-synchronous low Earth orbit throughout its mission. Its SEM-2 package measured precipitating and trapped energetic particles, auroral electrons/protons, and radiation-belt populations for space weather and geospace studies.

GOES-7 (launched 1987, operated until 1996) was a NOAA geostationary weather and space-environment satellite. It remained in geostationary Earth orbit but was relocated in longitude: initially serving GOES-West near 135°W, after GOES-6’s 1989 failure moved to a central/East coverage slot near 98°W through 1995, then backup service until decommissioning. Its Space Environment Monitor measured local magnetic field, energetic particles, and solar X-rays.

Rankin Inlet (IAGA code RIT) is a ground geomagnetic observatory at Rankin Inlet, Nunavut, Canada, with CDAWeb/INTERMAGNET records from at least the 2010s to present. It measures local vector geomagnetic-field variations for ionospheric current, auroral, and magnetospheric disturbance studies; it has no orbital phases.

Mount Wilson Observatory is a ground-based solar observatory on Mount Wilson, California, with solar operations beginning in 1908. Its 60-ft Solar Tower spectroheliograph provides synoptic full-disk chromospheric solar images, especially H-alpha and Ca II K, for studies of sunspots, plages, filaments, active regions, and long-term solar activity; it has no spacecraft orbit.

BARREL-1O was a NASA/Dartmouth stratospheric balloon payload flown during the first BARREL Antarctic campaign in 2013 (ended 2013), launched from Antarctica and drifting at roughly 30–40 km altitude over Antarctica/Southern Ocean rather than orbiting. It measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, with magnetic-field and GPS/ephemeris data.

Sanikiluaq Geophysical Observatory (Sanikiluaq, Nunavut, Canada; operational in CDAWeb at least from 2006) is a fixed ground-based high-latitude station in the Canadian/THEMIS-CARISMA geomagnetic network, measuring local magnetic-field variations for auroral ionosphere and magnetosphere studies; it has no orbital phases.

Yellowknife (YKC) is a fixed ground geomagnetic observatory near Yellowknife, Northwest Territories, Canada, operated in the Canadian/IAGA/INTERMAGNET networks since 1957 and still active. It has no orbit; it measures local vector magnetic-field variations for studies of ionospheric currents, magnetospheric disturbances, substorms, and auroral activity.

Vize Island Geophysical Observatory (IAGA VIZ; operating since at least 1957) is a fixed ground geomagnetic station on Vize Island in the Russian high Arctic (~79.5°N, 77°E). It has no orbit or relocations; magnetometers record local vector/scalar magnetic-field variations for polar-cap electrodynamics, magnetic storms, and space-weather studies.

Purcell Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based geomagnetic station at Purcell, Oklahoma, USA; its operational start/end dates are not confirmed here. It operates a magnetometer measuring local geomagnetic field variations used for ionospheric, magnetospheric, geomagnetic-storm, and space-weather studies; as a fixed ground site, it has no orbital phases.

NASA’s Pioneer 10 (launched 1972; routine mission ended 1997, last contact 2003) was a deep-space planetary and heliophysics probe. It cruised outward through the inner solar system and asteroid belt in 1972-73, flew through Jupiter’s magnetosphere during the Dec. 1973 flyby, then followed a solar-system escape trajectory through the outer heliosphere, measuring solar wind, magnetic fields, cosmic rays, and energetic particles.

BARREL-1S was a NASA Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses payload launched in 2013 for the Antarctic BARREL campaign and ended in 2013. It was not an orbiter: carried by a stratospheric balloon at roughly 30–40 km in the Antarctic polar vortex, it measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer/housekeeping context, in conjunction with the Van Allen Probes.

Ittoqqortoormiit (Scoresbysund) Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground station in East Greenland, operating since at least the early 1980s, with magnetometers measuring local geomagnetic field variations for high-latitude ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies; as a ground observatory it has no orbital phases.

Sept Iles Geophysical Observatory is a ground geomagnetic station at Sept-Îles, Quebec, Canada, operating since at least 1977, measuring local geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies. It is fixed on Earth; no orbital or vantage-point phases apply.

Solund Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground geomagnetic station at Solund on Norway’s west coast, operating since about 1996 with no orbital motion or relocation. It records local magnetic-field variations using a ground magnetometer for ionospheric, auroral-current, and magnetospheric studies, with data distributed through networks archived in CDAWeb.

Wallops Island Geophysical Observatory is a ground geomagnetic observatory at Wallops Island, Virginia, USA, using magnetometers to measure local magnetic-field variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies. It has no orbit; operational start/end dates are not specified in the provided CDAWeb/SPASE context.

LANL-2001 was a Los Alamos geosynchronous Earth-orbit spacecraft, operational in 2001-2008, with no major orbit changes; it sampled the near-equatorial magnetosphere at GEO. Its Magnetospheric Plasma Analyzer (MPA) measured 3D ion and electron energy-per-charge distributions for magnetospheric plasma and space-weather studies.

MMS-1, one of NASA’s four Magnetospheric Multiscale spacecraft (launched 2015, operating), studies magnetic reconnection, turbulence, and particle acceleration with high-rate fields and plasma instruments. It flew a highly elliptical Earth orbit with apogee near 12 RE in 2015-early 2017 for dayside magnetopause/near-tail campaigns; from 2017 its apogee was raised to about 25 RE for deeper magnetotail seasons while continuing magnetopause crossings.

International GNSS Service (IGS, operational from 1994) is a global ground-based network of continuously operating GNSS/GPS receivers and analysis centers, not a spacecraft. It provides precise satellite tracking, orbit and clock products for geodesy and positioning, and heliophysics users derive global/regional ionospheric total electron content and scintillation-related diagnostics from its worldwide stations.

Dead Horse Geophysical Observatory (operational by 2006 in CDAWeb/THEMIS-era holdings) is a fixed ground magnetometer station at Deadhorse/Prudhoe Bay, Alaska, not a spacecraft. It measures local vector geomagnetic field variations for auroral-zone, high-latitude ionosphere-magnetosphere, and space-weather studies.

Tromsø Magnetometer is a ground-based IAGA geomagnetic observatory at Tromsø, Norway (TRO; ~69.7°N, 19.0°E), operational since the 20th century, with digital CDAWeb-era data used for heliophysics. It measures local geomagnetic field variations from auroral electrojets, ionospheric currents, substorms, and geomagnetic storms; it has no orbital history.

ESA’s Cluster mission (launched 2000; science operations 2001-2024) was four spacecraft in coordinated highly elliptical polar Earth orbits, with varying spacecraft separations and evolving local-time coverage. It measured magnetospheric plasma, magnetic/electric fields, waves, and energetic particles in the magnetosphere, magnetosheath, bow shock, and sometimes upstream solar wind.

Munin was a Swedish microsatellite (launched 2000; science operations ended in 2001) in a low-Earth near-polar orbit throughout its mission, with no known major orbital relocation. It studied auroral and magnetospheric plasma processes, wave–particle interactions, and space weather; MEDUSA measured energetic neutral atoms and charged particles in near-Earth geospace.

The Tristan da Cunha Geophysical Observatory is a ground geomagnetic station on Tristan da Cunha in the South Atlantic, operational by at least the mid-20th century, with no spacecraft orbit. It measures geomagnetic field variations using magnetometers for solar-terrestrial physics, geomagnetic disturbance, and space-weather studies.

LANL-1997 was a Los Alamos National Laboratory geosynchronous Earth-orbit spacecraft operating from 1997 to 2008. Its vantage point remained near geosynchronous orbit, where MPA and SOPA measured magnetospheric plasma and energetic electron/ion populations for radiation-belt, plasma sheet, and space-weather studies.

ELFIN-B (Electron Losses and Fields Investigation B) was a UCLA/NASA 3U CubeSat launched in 2018 and operated until its 2022 decay/reentry in a single low-Earth, near-polar orbit with no major orbit changes beyond atmospheric decay. It measured radiation-belt electron and ion precipitation, pitch-angle distributions, and magnetic fields to study wave-particle loss into the atmosphere.

NASA’s Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS, launched 2013) is a Sun-pointing SMEX observatory in a near-polar, Sun-synchronous low-Earth orbit that has not changed over the mission. It studies the solar chromosphere and transition region with high-resolution ultraviolet spectroscopy and slit-jaw imaging, probing mass and energy flow between the photosphere and corona.

Fort Churchill Geophysical Observatory (established for the IGY in 1957) is a ground geophysical/magnetic station at or near Churchill, Manitoba, Canada, not a spacecraft. It measures local geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for auroral-zone ionospheric currents, substorms, and geomagnetic-storm studies; CDAWeb holdings may represent only specific instrument campaigns.

Tartu Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetic observatory at Tõravere near Tartu, Estonia, operational since 1964 and still active. It has no orbit or changing vantage point; its magnetometers record local geomagnetic-field variations used for ionospheric, magnetospheric, geophysical, and space-weather studies.

Hankasalmi (HAN), operational in the IMAGE ground magnetometer network since the 1990s, is a fixed IAGA station at Hankasalmi, Finland (~62.3°N, 26.6°E). It measures three-component geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric current, auroral electrojet, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling studies; it has no orbital phases.

The Kaktovik Geophysical Observatory is a fixed Arctic ground station at Kaktovik/Barter Island on Alaska’s North Slope, operating at least by 1995 with no known end date. Its fluxgate magnetometer records local geomagnetic-field variations at auroral latitudes for studies of ionospheric currents, magnetospheric disturbances, substorms, and space weather.

Equator-S was a German-led magnetospheric spacecraft launched in 1997 and operated until 1998. It flew a fixed, highly elliptical, low-inclination near-equatorial Earth orbit, about 500 km perigee to 67,000 km apogee, to study the dayside magnetosphere, magnetopause, and equatorial boundary regions using magnetic/electric fields, plasma, energetic-particle, and wave measurements.

Amderma (IAGA code AMD) is a fixed high-latitude ground geomagnetic observatory at Amderma, Russia, with IAGA records beginning around the 1957 IGY. It measures time variations of the local magnetic field for auroral, ionospheric, and magnetospheric current-system studies; it has no orbital phases.
NOAA GOES geostationary satellite series as a whole (all satellites combined); represents GOES observations not attributed to one specific GOES satellite number.

IAGA Sitka (SIT) is a ground geomagnetic observatory operating at Sitka, Alaska since 1901. It has no orbit; it records local vector magnetic-field components and variations for studies of geomagnetic storms, auroral electrojets, and ionospheric/magnetospheric current systems as part of the global IAGA/INTERMAGNET observatory network.

NOAA-19 (NOAA-N Prime), launched in 2009, is a NOAA POES meteorological and space-weather satellite operating in near-polar, Sun-synchronous low Earth orbit at about 850 km; it has had no major orbital relocation beyond normal orbital/local-time drift. Its SEM-2 package measures energetic electrons and protons, auroral precipitation, radiation-belt particles, and solar proton events in near-Earth geospace.

ISEE 1 (International Sun-Earth Explorer 1, 1977-1987) was a NASA magnetospheric spacecraft. It remained in a highly elliptical geocentric orbit, with apogee about 23 Earth radii and low perigee, sampling the solar wind, bow shock, magnetopause, magnetosheath, magnetotail, and inner magnetosphere with plasma, magnetic-field, energetic-particle, and wave instruments.

NASA’s POLAR spacecraft (1996-2008) studied Earth’s polar magnetosphere, aurora, plasma, fields, waves, and energetic particles. It remained in a highly elliptical, near-polar geocentric orbit (about 1.8 by 9 Earth radii, 18-hr period); orbital precession shifted apogee viewing/coverage through different polar and magnetospheric regions over the mission.

Ulysses was a joint ESA/NASA mission (1990-2009) studying the heliosphere in 3D. After launch it cruised in the ecliptic to Jupiter, making a February 1992 Jovian flyby with magnetospheric science, then entered a high-inclination heliocentric orbit for solar polar passes in 1994-95, 2000-01, and 2006-08, measuring solar wind plasma/composition, fields, energetic particles, and radio/plasma waves.

NASA’s Transition Region and Coronal Explorer (TRACE; launched 1998, operated until 2010) was a solar SMEX observatory in a near-circular, Sun-synchronous low-Earth polar orbit throughout its mission. It obtained high-resolution normal-incidence EUV, UV, and white-light images of the solar transition region and corona, studying coronal loops, active regions, flares, and solar magnetic dynamics.

LANL-1990 was a Los Alamos National Laboratory geosynchronous spacecraft operating from 1990 to 2004. It remained in geosynchronous Earth orbit and carried MPA and SOPA instruments to measure magnetospheric plasma and energetic particle populations, supporting studies of the radiation belts, ring current, substorms, and space weather.

BARREL-1J was a NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses high-altitude balloon payload flown over Antarctica during the first BARREL campaign in 2013, ending that year. It drifted in the stratospheric polar vortex and measured bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with supporting magnetometer and GPS/housekeeping data.

Hi-C (High-resolution Coronal Imager) is a NASA sounding-rocket solar observatory, not an orbital spacecraft; it makes brief suborbital flights from White Sands Missile Range. Hi-C flew on 11 Jul 2012, obtaining ~5 min of ultra-high-resolution 193 Å EUV coronal images; Hi-C 2.1 flew on 29 May 2018 at 172 Å; Hi-C Flare flew on 17 Apr 2024 for flare/coronal EUV imaging.

Pueblo Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetic observatory in Pueblo, Colorado, USA; its exact operational start/end dates are not confidently identified here. It provides fixed-site magnetometer measurements of local geomagnetic field variations for heliophysics, geomagnetic-storm, and ionospheric-current studies, with no orbital or relocation phases.

Interball-1 (Tail Probe) was a Russian-led heliophysics spacecraft (1995-2000) that studied solar wind–magnetosphere coupling, plasma waves, particles and fields in the bow shock, magnetosheath, magnetopause and magnetotail. It remained in a highly elliptical geocentric orbit throughout the mission (about 1,000 x 190,000 km, ~63° inclination, ~4-day period), with apogee precession sampling different local times.

RBSP-B (Van Allen Probe B), launched in 2012 and operated until July 2019, studied Earth’s radiation belts and inner magnetosphere with energetic-particle, fields, and wave instruments. It flew a near-equatorial, highly elliptical geocentric orbit from 2012 to early 2019; in 2019 disposal maneuvers lowered perigee before shutdown, while observations continued.

Fort Smith (FSM) is a ground geomagnetic observatory at Fort Smith, Northwest Territories, Canada, operated since about 1972 as part of the Canadian/IAGA geomagnetic network. It has no orbit; it records vector and scalar geomagnetic-field variations for studies of ionospheric and magnetospheric currents, storms, and substorms.

Leirvogur (LRV) is an IAGA ground magnetic observatory in southwest Iceland near Reykjavík, in continuous operation since 1957. It measures local vector geomagnetic field variations and high-latitude magnetic disturbances for ionospheric, magnetospheric, auroral electrojet, and global geomagnetic monitoring studies.

Goose Bay Geophysical Observatory (operational by at least 1990; exact start/end not confirmed here) is a fixed ground magnetometer station at Goose Bay, Labrador, Canada, measuring geomagnetic field variations for auroral/subauroral current studies and regional/global geomagnetic monitoring; it has no orbital or relocation phases.

BARREL-2C was a NASA/Dartmouth BARREL balloon payload operated during the second Antarctic campaign in the 2013-2014 austral season, ending in 2014. It was not in space orbit; it drifted in the Antarctic stratosphere with circumpolar winds, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation plus magnetic field and GPS ephemeris for magnetospheric space-weather studies.

THEMIS-C (launched 2007), later ARTEMIS-P2, carries plasma, energetic-particle, field and wave instruments for magnetospheric and lunar/heliospheric science. From 2007-2010 it flew a highly elliptical Earth orbit as an outer THEMIS probe sampling the magnetotail and inner magnetosphere; in 2010-2011 it used lunar flybys and Earth-Moon Lagrange transfer orbits, then from 2011 onward has orbited the Moon.

Dynamics Explorer 1 (DE 1, NASA Explorer 62; 1981-1991) flew a highly elliptical near-polar Earth orbit, about 570 x 23,000 km, sampling the magnetosphere, plasmasphere, auroral regions, and topside ionosphere. It measured fields, plasma waves, ion/electron populations, ion drift, neutral/auroral emissions, and global auroral images to study magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling.

NASA’s Pioneer Venus Orbiter (Pioneer 12; launched 1978, operated at Venus 1978–1992) studied Venus’s atmosphere, ionosphere, induced magnetosphere, and solar-wind interaction. It remained in a highly elliptical, near-polar ~24-h Venus orbit, with low-periapsis aeronomy passes and distant apoapsis/wake sampling, until atmospheric entry in 1992.

Petersburg Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based geomagnetic station in St. Petersburg, Russia, operating at least during the CDAWeb digital data era (1990s–present; exact start not verified here). It measures local geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies; it has no orbital phases.

Arctic Village Magnetometer (AVI), operational at least by 1995 and ongoing, is a ground geomagnetic station at Arctic Village, Alaska (~68.1°N, 145.6°W). It has no orbit; it measures local magnetic-field variations and disturbances for auroral ionosphere, magnetosphere, and space-weather studies, with IAGA/CDAWeb data.

Americus Geophysical Observatory (operational in CDAWeb ground-magnetometer records from about 2005/2006 onward; end date not confirmed) is a fixed station in Americus, Georgia, USA. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for heliophysics studies of ionospheric and magnetospheric currents, geomagnetic storms, substorms, and ULF waves; its location has not changed.

NASA’s IMAGE (Imager for Magnetopause-to-Aurora Global Exploration, 2000-2005) was a spin-stabilized spacecraft in a highly elliptical near-polar Earth orbit throughout its science mission, enabling global magnetospheric imaging. It observed the plasmasphere, ring current, aurora, magnetopause, and cusp using FUV/EUV imagers, energetic neutral atom imagers, and the Radio Plasma Imager.

Pello Geophysical Observatory (PEL; operating since 1973) is a fixed ground-based magnetometer station at Pello, northern Finland, now part of the IMAGE magnetometer network. It records geomagnetic field variations used to study ionospheric currents, auroral electrojets, geomagnetic pulsations, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling; its observing location has not changed.

DMSP F16 was a U.S. Air Force DMSP 5D-3 spacecraft launched in 2003 and operated until 2020 in a near-circular, Sun-synchronous polar low-Earth orbit at about 830–850 km altitude; its orbit type did not change. It provided operational meteorological and space-weather measurements of the high-latitude ionosphere/aurora, including SSJ precipitating particles, ionospheric plasma, and magnetic-field data.

Park Site Geophysical Observatory is a ground magnetometer site at Park Site, Antarctica; its operational start and end years are not confidently documented in the provided registry context. It records geomagnetic field variations for studies of high-latitude ionospheric currents, auroral electrodynamics, and magnetospheric disturbances.

BARREL-2D was a specific Balloon Array for RBSP Relativistic Electron Losses payload flown in the second Antarctic campaign (2013-2014). It was a high-altitude, long-duration stratospheric balloon over Antarctica, not an orbital spacecraft, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, with GPS/ephemeris and magnetic-field context for Van Allen Probes conjunction studies.

Roemoe is a ground geophysical observatory on Rømø, Denmark, measuring local geomagnetic field variations with a magnetometer for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and geomagnetic studies; it is fixed at this ground site, with no orbital phases. Its precise operational start/end years are not confirmed here, so use CDAWeb/SPASE metadata for dataset-specific coverage.

Sørøya Geophysical Observatory (SOR) is a fixed ground magnetic observatory on Sørøya, northern Norway, in operation by at least the CDAWeb data era; it has no orbital phases. It records geomagnetic field variations with magnetometers for auroral-zone ionospheric, magnetospheric, and geomagnetic-disturbance studies.

Attu Geophysical Observatory (ATU) was a USGS ground magnetic observatory on Attu Island in the Aleutian Islands, Alaska, operated in the mid-20th century and represented in CDAWeb for geomagnetic field time series. It measured high-latitude magnetic variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, auroral, and geomagnetic storm studies; it had no orbital motion.

Qaanaaq Geophysical Observatory is a fixed high-latitude ground station at Qaanaaq, northwest Greenland, operating since at least the CDAWeb data era to record geomagnetic field variations with a fluxgate magnetometer for polar ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies; it has no orbital or relocation phases.

Athabasca Geophysical Observatory is a ground station at Athabasca, Alberta, Canada, used in heliophysics observations from at least the THEMIS ground-based era (2006 onward). It has no orbit; it records local geomagnetic field variations with a fluxgate magnetometer for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies.

THEMIS Ground CANMAG ATHA is the Athabasca, Alberta, Canada station of the THEMIS/Canadian ground magnetometer network, operational in CDAWeb from 2007 and continuing. It measures ground vector geomagnetic-field variations supporting studies of auroral currents, substorms, ULF waves, and magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling with THEMIS spacecraft.

SUNRISE-1 was a stratospheric balloon solar observatory on a single June 2009 flight, launched from ESRANGE near Kiruna, Sweden, and drifting west across the Arctic at about 35–37 km before recovery in northern Canada. It observed photospheric and chromospheric fine structure and magnetic fields at high spatial resolution, using instruments such as SuFI and IMaX.

NASA’s Genesis mission (2001-2004) studied solar wind composition and returned collected ions to Earth. After launch it transferred to the Sun-Earth L1 region, operating in a halo orbit there from late 2001 to April 2004; it then departed L1 for an Earth-return trajectory, releasing its sample capsule in September 2004. GIM and GEM measured solar wind ions and electrons.

McGrath Geophysical Observatory is a fixed ground magnetometer station at McGrath, Alaska, operational in CDAWeb at least in the THEMIS/ground-magnetometer era from the mid-2000s onward. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for studies of auroral-zone ionospheric currents, substorms, and magnetospheric dynamics; its vantage point does not change.

NOAA-15 (launched 1998; SEM-2 space-environment data commonly used through 2020) was a NOAA POES polar weather satellite in near-circular, near-polar Sun-synchronous low Earth orbit throughout its mission, with only normal local-time drift. Its SEM-2 package, including TED and MEPED, measured auroral particles, radiation-belt electrons/protons, and solar energetic particles.

St. John’s (STJ) is an IAGA/INTERMAGNET ground magnetometer observatory at St. John’s, Newfoundland, Canada, operational by 1968 and still active. It has no orbit; from its fixed North Atlantic site it records geomagnetic field components and variations used for ionospheric, magnetospheric, auroral, and space-weather studies.

BARREL-1U was an individual NASA/Dartmouth Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses payload, operated in 2013 during the first Antarctic BARREL campaign. It flew as a long-duration stratospheric balloon over Antarctica and the Southern Ocean, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays/gamma rays and magnetic field signatures of radiation-belt electron precipitation, often coordinated with Van Allen Probes.

Mekrijärvi Geophysical Observatory is a ground geomagnetic station at Ilomantsi, eastern Finland, operating since at least the early 1990s in the IMAGE magnetometer network. It measures local geomagnetic field variations for auroral electrojet, ionospheric current, magnetic-pulsation, and magnetospheric studies; it has no orbital phases.

TWINS-1, a NASA mission-of-opportunity payload launched in 2006 on the USA-184/NROL-22 spacecraft, operated for heliophysics science from 2008 to 2020. Its orbit did not change: a 12-hour, highly elliptical Molniya-type Earth orbit at about 63° inclination, giving high-latitude apogee views of the magnetosphere. It used wide-angle energetic neutral atom imagers and Lyman-alpha sensors to study the ring current, geocorona, and global magnetospheric dynamics.

SATech-01, launched in 2022, is a Chinese solar remote-sensing satellite in low Earth Sun-synchronous orbit; no major orbital phase changes are reported. Its Solar Upper Transition Region Imager (SUTRI) takes full-disk extreme-ultraviolet images, especially around 46.5 nm, to study the Sun’s upper chromosphere, transition region, corona, and space-weather-relevant activity.

BARREL-2Y was a NASA high-altitude balloon payload flown over Antarctica in the 2014 BARREL second campaign, not an orbital spacecraft. It drifted in the stratospheric polar vortex at roughly 30–40 km altitude, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays from radiation-belt electron precipitation, with magnetometer and GPS context, coordinated with Van Allen Probes.

FOXSI-3, the third Focusing Optics X-ray Solar Imager sounding-rocket flight, operated only during a suborbital solar observing flight from White Sands Missile Range on 2018-09-07. It flew above the atmosphere for minutes, not into orbit, using grazing-incidence focusing optics and X-ray detectors to image solar hard X-ray emission from active regions, microflares, and flares.

NOAA GOES-11 (launched 2000; operational GOES service 2006-2011) was a geostationary Earth-orbit weather satellite carrying space-weather sensors for solar X-rays, energetic particles, and the local geomagnetic field. It remained in geostationary orbit as an on-orbit spare before becoming GOES-West near 135°W in 2006; it was retired to graveyard orbit in December 2011.

ESA’s Rosetta spacecraft (launched 2004, ended 2016) studied comet 67P and its plasma, dust, gas, and nucleus. It cruised heliocentrically with Earth flybys in 2005/2007/2009, a Mars flyby in 2007, and asteroid flybys Šteins 2008 and Lutetia 2010; after 2011-14 hibernation it rendezvoused with 67P in Aug 2014, escorting it through perihelion until Sep 2016.

Dikson Geophysical Observatory is a high-latitude Arctic ground station at Dikson, Russia, established in 1933 and used for geomagnetic monitoring rather than spaceflight. It records ground magnetic-field variations with magnetometers to study auroral-zone ionospheric currents, geomagnetic storms, substorms, and magnetospheric dynamics.

Qeqertarsuaq Geophysical Observatory, formerly Godhavn/GDH, is a ground geomagnetic station at Qeqertarsuaq on Disko Island, Greenland, where magnetic observations began in 1926 and continue today. It has no orbit; its magnetometers measure local geomagnetic-field variations for auroral electrojet, ionospheric current, and magnetospheric disturbance studies.

Honolulu Geophysical Observatory (HON), operating since 1902, is a fixed ground geomagnetic observatory on Oahu near Honolulu, Hawaii. It has no orbital phases; magnetometers record local vector/scalar geomagnetic field variations and disturbances for ionospheric, magnetospheric, space-weather, and secular-variation studies, with data distributed via systems such as CDAWeb.

THEMIS-D (launched 2007) is one of NASA’s THEMIS probes studying terrestrial substorms, magnetotail dynamics, plasma, fields, and energetic particles. After commissioning and orbit raising in 2007 it has remained a near-equatorial, highly elliptical Earth orbiting inner THEMIS probe, with roughly 1-day geocentric orbits and apogee near the magnetosphere/magnetotail; it did not transfer to lunar ARTEMIS orbit.

The Ivalo magnetometer (IVA), operational in IMAGE/CDAWeb records from at least 1994, is a fixed ground station near Ivalo, northern Finland, measuring geomagnetic field variations for auroral, ionospheric, and magnetospheric studies. It is part of the IMAGE high-latitude magnetometer network and contributes IAGA-style ground magnetic data.

Solar Flare Telescope (SFT, operational from 1990) is a ground-based solar observatory at the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan in Mitaka, Tokyo. It observes the full solar disk, chiefly in H-alpha, to study chromospheric flares, filaments, prominences, and eruption morphology; it also supports photospheric magnetic-field context for solar activity studies.

Narsarsuaq Geophysical Observatory (NAQ), operating since the IGY era (about 1957), is a ground station in southern Greenland near 61.2°N, 45.4°W. It has no orbit; it records local geomagnetic-field variations with magnetometers for ionospheric, auroral, and magnetospheric studies and contributes to Greenland/high-latitude monitoring networks.

The John W. Evans Solar Facility at Sacramento Peak/Sunspot, New Mexico, is a ground-based NSO solar observatory that began operation in 1952. Its spectroheliograph/coronagraph observations provide narrowband full-disk and off-limb solar images of the chromosphere, photosphere, and corona for studies of solar atmospheric structure and activity; no orbital phase applies.

BARREL-1T was a Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses test high-altitude balloon payload, operated during the 2008-2009 Antarctic long-duration balloon season and ending in 2009. It was not in orbit; it floated in the stratosphere over Antarctica/Southern Ocean on circumpolar winds, measuring bremsstrahlung X-rays/gamma rays and magnetic perturbations from radiation-belt electron precipitation.

Baker Lake (IAGA code BLC) is a ground-based geomagnetic observatory at Baker Lake, Nunavut, Canada, operating in the IAGA/CDAWeb record since at least the late 1950s. It measures local vector geomagnetic field variations for auroral-zone, magnetospheric, ionospheric, and geomagnetic-storm studies; its location has no orbital phases.

Owens Valley Radio Observatory is a Caltech ground-based radio facility near Big Pine, California, operating since 1956. For heliophysics it hosts the Owens Valley Solar Array, expanded as EOVSA in 2017, which makes solar microwave/radio interferometric images and spectra for studies of flares, coronal magnetic fields, and energetic electrons.

Ny-Ålesund (NAL) is a fixed ground geomagnetic observatory at Ny-Ålesund, Svalbard, Norway, operational in space-physics archives from at least 1993 and continuing. Its magnetometer records local high-latitude geomagnetic field variations near cusp/polar-cap footprints for studies of ionospheric currents, substorms, and magnetospheric disturbances.

Igloolik Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based geomagnetic station at Igloolik, Nunavut, Canada, operational from at least the early 1990s, with no well-documented end year in the registry. It has no orbit; it records local magnetic-field variations for high-latitude ionospheric, auroral, cusp, and magnetospheric studies.

Donna Geophysical Observatory is a ground-based geomagnetic observatory at Donna, Texas, USA, operating magnetometers to record local geomagnetic field variations for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and geomagnetic studies; it has no orbital phases. Its exact operational start/end dates for CDAWeb/SPASE use are not confirmed here.

Victoria (VIC) is an IAGA/Canadian ground geomagnetic observatory operating in Victoria, British Columbia, Canada since 1957. It has no orbit; it records local vector magnetic-field variations and geomagnetic indices/measurements used for ionospheric, magnetospheric, and space-weather studies, with data distributed through systems including CDAWeb.

It obtained full-disk photospheric magnetic-field and Doppler measurements plus chromospheric and spectral irradiance observations with VSM, ISS, and Full Disk Patrol.

instruments.description: GOES Space Environment Monitor (SEM) — generic across the GOES series (any satellite). The SEM package carries the X-Ray Sensor (XRS, soft/hard solar X-ray irradiance), Energetic Particle Sensor (EPS: electrons, protons, alphas) and a magnetometer (MAG). Use for a GOES X-ray / particle / magnetic-field mention that does not name a specific GOES satellite number.

Parker Solar Probe SPAN-A (Solar Probe Analyzer A; houses the ram-side ion analyzer SPAN-Ai, also designated SPAN-I or SPAN-Ion (Livi et al. 2022), and the ram-side electron analyzer SPAN-Ae) electrostatic analyzer pair measuring ram-side ion and electron velocity distributions; one of the SWEAP (Solar Wind Electrons Alphas and Protons) suite sensors alongside the SPC (Solar Probe Cup) and SPAN-B (Solar Probe Analyzer B), with ions from several eV/q to 20 keV/q using time-of-flight mass/charge discrimination and electrons from several eV to 20 keV

Parker Solar Probe SPAN-B (Solar Probe Analyzer B) electrostatic analyzer measuring anti-ram solar-wind electron velocity distributions from several eV to 20 keV; the electron-only sensor of the SWEAP (Solar Wind Electrons Alphas and Protons) suite alongside SPC (Solar Probe Cup) and SPAN-A (Solar Probe Analyzer A); together with SPAN-A's electron analyzer SPAN-Ae it constitutes the SPAN electron measurement, also designated SPAN-E or SPAN-Electron (Whittlesey et al. 2020), paired with SPAN-A electron coverage for near-4π electron fields of view excluding the heat shield.

CLASP2 (Chromospheric LAyer SpectroPolarimeter 2) Spectropolarimeter1 ultraviolet spectropolarimeter channel measuring solar chromospheric Stokes I, Q, U, V profiles near 280 nm, especially Mg II k 279.6 nm, Mg II h 280.4 nm, and Mn I 280.2 nm; one of the CLASP2 sounding-rocket 2019 spectropolarimeter channels alongside Spectropolarimeter2 and the slit-jaw imager

Hinode EIS (EUV Imaging Spectrometer) slit/slot EUV imaging spectrograph measuring solar transition-region and coronal emission-line intensities, Doppler shifts, line widths, temperatures and densities in two wavelength bands, 170-210 Å and 250-290 Å, using narrow slits and wide slots for rastered spectra and monochromatic images

instruments.instrument_name: Full longwave EUV observation of Sun with EUNIS (2006 flight)
instruments.description: EUNIS-06 EUNIS (Extreme Ultraviolet Normal-Incidence Spectrograph) sounding-rocket EUV imaging spectrograph measuring spatially resolved solar transition-region and coronal emission lines; 2006 flight long-wavelength channel provided full-Sun/solar-target spectra over ~300–370 Å, alongside the short-wavelength channel covering ~170–205 Å for cross-calibration and plasma diagnostics

instruments.instrument_name: Shortwave EUV observation of Sun with EUNIS (2006 flight)
instruments.description: EUNIS 2006 SW (Extreme Ultraviolet Normal-Incidence Spectrograph short-wavelength) normal-incidence solar EUV imaging spectrograph channel measuring transition-region and coronal emission-line spectra over ~170–205 Å; one of the 2006 EUNIS sounding-rocket channels alongside the LW long-wavelength channel (~300–370 Å)

instruments.instrument_name: Shortwave EUV observation of Sun with EUNIS (trimmed/2006 flight)

GOES-17 (2018–2023) GOES-R Series Solar Ultraviolet Imager (SUVI) of Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite 17 (GOES-R Series 17; GOES-S/GOES17), full-disk extreme-ultraviolet solar telescope measuring chromospheric and coronal emission in six passbands centered at 94, 131, 171, 195, 284, and 304 Å for flares, active regions, coronal holes, and eruptions; launched in 2018.

Mauna Loa Solar Observatory Mk4 (Mark IV) K-coronameter white-light coronagraph measuring polarized brightness (pB) of the K-corona from Thomson-scattered photospheric light, used to derive low-coronal electron density and track coronal mass ejections over roughly 1.14-2.86 solar radii in broadband visible/near-infrared observations

SOHO UVCS (Ultraviolet Coronagraph Spectrometer) ultraviolet coronagraph spectrometer measuring extended-corona ultraviolet line intensities, profiles, Doppler shifts, and widths from ~1.5–10 solar radii; covers H I Ly-α 1216 Å, Ly-β 1025 Å, O VI 1032/1037 Å, and coronal lines such as Si XII 499/521 Å, with a visible-light channel for polarized K-corona brightness/density

Focusing Optics X-ray Solar Imager FOXSI flight #1 (flight 1, 2012-11-02) sounding-rocket hard-X-ray focusing solar telescope measuring coronal X-ray photons for imaging spectroscopy of active regions, microflares, and flares, using seven grazing-incidence Wolter-I optics modules focused onto silicon strip detectors over ~4–15 keV; launched 2012-11-02

ACE SWICS (Solar Wind Ion Composition Spectrometer) electrostatic-analyzer/time-of-flight ion mass spectrometer measuring solar-wind and pickup-ion elemental abundances, ionic charge states, mass, density, bulk speed and temperature for major ions H-Fe; covers 0.11-66.7 keV/q (about 35-600 keV total ion energy) with full composition scans about every 12-13 min, often cited with companion SWIMS (Solar Wind Ion Mass Spectrometer)

BARREL (Balloon Array for Radiation Belt Relativistic Electron Losses) Balloon 1K DPU (Data Processing Unit) flight computer and telemetry platform for payload 1K of the first Antarctic campaign (2012-2013), acquiring and framing XRI (X-ray instrument) spectrometer, magnetometer, GPS, and EDI (Engineering Data Interface) data for Iridium downlink and command-cutdown control

STEREO-B PLASTIC (PLasma And SupraThermal Ion Composition) time-of-flight mass spectrometer and electrostatic analyzer measuring solar wind and suprathermal ions, including H–Fe elemental composition, mass/charge and charge states, and proton/alpha density, velocity and temperature, over roughly 0.3–80 keV/e in the STEREO-B in-situ particle payload

BARREL (Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses) Balloon 1B DPU (Data Processing Unit) platform data-handling unit acquiring and framing XRI (X-ray instrument), magnetometer, GPS, and EDI (Engineering Data Interface) data for Iridium downlink; payload 1B of the first Antarctic balloon campaign (2012-2013), not a science sensor itself

STEREO-A PLASTIC (PLasma And SupraThermal Ion Composition) solar wind ion composition/mass spectrometer in the STEREO heliospheric in-situ payload measuring protons, alpha particles, heavy-ion charge states, elemental composition, bulk solar wind properties/plasma moments, and suprathermal ion fluxes from ~0.3 to 80 keV/e (keV/q), including H, He, C, O, Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe

STEREO-A S/WAVES (Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory/WAVES; SWAVES) radio and plasma wave investigation measuring solar and interplanetary radio burst spectra, interplanetary Langmuir waves, and in situ electric-field wave spectra from 2.5 kHz to 16 MHz; comprising Low Frequency Receiver (LFR), High Frequency Receiver (HFR), Fixed Frequency Receiver (FFR), and Time Domain Sampler (TDS) using three electric monopole antennas for direction finding and burst tracking

BARREL Balloon 1C MAG (Magnetometer) TCM2 (Tilt Compensated Magnetometer) three-axis magnetometer measuring vector magnetic-field components at 1 s cadence with ~10 nT resolution for substorm and ultra-low-frequency (ULF) wave context; payload 1C of the first BARREL Antarctic balloon campaign (2012-2013), conjugate with the Van Allen Probes

BARREL Balloon 1O XRI (X-ray Instrument) energetic particle/X-ray scintillator spectrometer measuring bremsstrahlung X-ray flux and spectra from precipitating radiation-belt electrons, 10 keV-10 MeV; payload 1O of the second BARREL Antarctic balloon campaign (2013-2014), with 50 ms bands at 10-180, 180-550, 550-840, and 840-1500 keV plus 48/256-channel spectra from 20 keV-7 MeV

BARREL (Balloon Array for Radiation-belt Relativistic Electron Losses) Balloon 1G XRI (X-ray Instrument) energetic-particle X-ray scintillator spectrometer measuring bremsstrahlung X-ray spectra and flux from precipitating radiation-belt electrons; payload 1G of the first Antarctic campaign (2012-2013), with 10 keV-10 MeV response, 50 ms rates in 10-180, 180-550, 550-840, and 840-1500 keV bands, plus 48/256-channel 20 keV-7 MeV spectra
